11. Stochastic Volatility Models and Model-Risk-Aware Option Relative Value

Main things we build in this project:

  • A clean SPX option modeling panel, reusing the option-chain, forward, IV, and Greek machinery from the earlier option projects without re-teaching those pieces.
  • A sequence of smile and stochastic-volatility models: SVI, SSVI, SABR, Merton jump-diffusion, Heston, and Bates.
  • A model comparison layer that separates fast surface fit, global surface discipline, stochastic dynamics, jump-tail behavior, runtime, Monte Carlo noise, and parameter warnings.
  • A model-risk-aware fair-value engine that turns fitted surfaces into residual scores only when pricing error, bid-ask uncertainty, and model disagreement leave enough room.
  • A next-day validation test that checks whether residuals have any forward information after hedging and costs.
  • A scheduled delta-hedged trading experiment comparing model-selected residual trades against matched ATM-style baseline trades.
  • A secondary BTC implementation using the library, where the same model stack faces a market with much wider smiles, rougher liquidity, and 24/7 trading.

The main story is different ways of explaining the same implied-volatility surface.

A surface model says, “give me today’s market quotes and I’ll draw a smooth smile.”
A stochastic volatility model says, “give me a stochastic process for the underlying and its variance, and I’ll generate option prices from the distribution of future outcomes.”
A jump model adds the idea that part of the smile comes from discontinuous moves that a continuous diffusion can’t reproduce efficiently.

We already spent earlier option projects on Black-Scholes/Black-76, implied-volatility inversion, Greeks, and surface/local-vol construction. Here we treat those as tools. The new work is the model layer above the surface: how each model encodes skew, convexity, tails, uncertainty, and tradability.

The goal isn’t only to find the smallest calibration error. We want to know which model errors are economically meaningful, which are just quote noise, which are too expensive to trade, and which survive a hedged next-day test.

1) The Unified Story: Surface Shape, Dynamics, and Trading Use

There are three layers of volatility modeling in this project, and keeping them separate makes the whole project easier to understand.

Layer A: quoted implied volatility

The market gives us option prices. After cleaning and IV inversion, we can write the quote as a point on a surface:

\[ (k,T,\sigma_{imp}) \]

where \(k=\log(K/F)\) is log-forward moneyness and \(T\) is time to expiry. This is the descriptive layer. It tells us what the market is charging today.

Layer B: model-generated fair value

A model produces its own price or volatility:

\[ V_i^{model} \quad \text{or} \quad \sigma_i^{model} \]

and we compare that against the quote. This is the calibration layer. SVI, SSVI, and SABR mostly live here as fast surface/smile explanations. Merton, Heston, and Bates also live here, but they generate prices through a distributional story.

Layer C: trade validation

A residual becomes useful only if it has forward information after costs:

\[ e_i=V_i^{model}-V_i^{mkt} \]

If \(e_i\) is positive, the model says the option is cheap. If \(e_i\) is negative, it says the option is rich. But that residual still has to survive bid-ask, model disagreement, hedge cost, and next-day validation.

This creates the project’s full logic:

\[ \text{market quotes} \rightarrow \text{surface/statistical model} \rightarrow \text{fair value residual} \rightarrow \text{validated hedged P\&L} \]

The reason this project is impressive is that it doesn’t stop at calibration. Many volatility projects end after fitting a smile and showing a nice plot. Here we ask a harder question: if a model says a quote is wrong, can we use that information in a scheduled hedged experiment?

Model Families in One Map

The six models can be organized by what they believe the source of the smile is.

Family Models here Main belief about smile
Static smile geometry SVI, SSVI The surface shape can be parameterized directly in \(k\) and \(T\)
Approximate stochastic smile SABR Volatility is random and correlated with the forward, but we use a fast IV approximation
Jump distribution Merton Tail prices come from rare discontinuous moves
Continuous stochastic variance Heston Tail prices and skew come from random mean-reverting variance
Hybrid jump + variance Bates Both stochastic variance and discontinuous jumps are needed

This taxonomy prevents confusion later. SVI can beat Heston on RMSE because it is designed to fit the observed smile directly. That doesn’t mean SVI gives a better scenario generator. Heston can have worse fit but a richer path story. Bates can improve the stochastic fit but become harder to identify.

So the practical question becomes: which role do we need?

  • For daily fair-value residuals, we need tight, stable cross-sectional pricing.
  • For understanding tail mechanisms, we need jump and stochastic-volatility diagnostics.
  • For avoiding false trades, we need model disagreement and uncertainty filters.
  • For backtesting, we need a hedged P&L workflow that doesn’t assume calibration error is automatically tradable.

This is the unified story of the whole project.

Surface Fit Versus Path Consistency

A surface model and a path model answer different technical questions.

A surface model is cross-sectional. It asks:

\[ (k,T)\mapsto \sigma_{imp}(k,T) \]

The fitted object is a map across strikes and maturities at one date. It can be extremely accurate because it is built to match the observed surface.

A path model is distributional. It asks for a stochastic law:

\[ F_0 \rightarrow F_T \]

or, with stochastic variance:

\[ (F_0,v_0)\rightarrow (F_T,v_T) \]

The option price then comes from the implied terminal payoff distribution:

\[ V=D\,E^Q[g(F_T)] \]

Path consistency is valuable because the same process can price many payoffs, simulate scenarios, compute path-dependent risks, and connect smile shape to forward dynamics. But a low-dimensional path model may fail to match every quote on one surface.

This is why the project doesn’t treat calibration RMSE as the only truth. A static model can fit today’s surface beautifully but say little about tomorrow’s smile dynamics. A path model can teach us about skew, jumps, and variance clustering while still losing the fit contest.

1) Reused Data and the New Modeling Target

We use the same SPX option-chain setting as the earlier option projects, so the raw data story stays short. The reproducibility layer is folder-based:

  • SPX option-chain source and builder: data/spx_optionsdx
  • U.S. Treasury yield source and downloader: data/us_treasury_yields
  • Project-wide data instructions: data folder

The option-chain cleaning, put-call parity forward inference, Black-76 implied-volatility inversion, and Greek computation have already been covered before. We only remind the minimum structure needed for the models in this project.

At every quote we need:

  • option type: call or put,
  • strike \(K\),
  • expiry time \(T\),
  • discount factor \(D(T)\),
  • forward price \(F_t(T)\),
  • mid, bid, ask, and bid-ask spread,
  • implied volatility \(\sigma_{imp}\),
  • log-forward moneyness \(k=\log(K/F_t)\),
  • Greek-based sensitivity, especially vega.

The pricing object underneath most of the project is the forward-discounted risk-neutral expectation:

\[ C_t(K,T)=D(t,T)\,E_t^Q[(F_T-K)^+] \]

and for puts:

\[ P_t(K,T)=D(t,T)\,E_t^Q[(K-F_T)^+] \]

Here \(E_t^Q[\cdot]\) means expectation under the risk-neutral pricing measure, not under the real-world return distribution. That distinction matters because the models are calibrated to option prices, not to historical SPX returns. If the market charges a volatility risk premium or jump risk premium, the calibrated parameters reflect the pricing distribution the market implies.

Risk-Neutral Model Parameters Versus Real-World Volatility

A common beginner mistake is to read calibrated option-model parameters as direct historical forecasts. We’ll avoid that. In this project, parameters are fitted to option prices, so they live under the risk-neutral measure \(Q\).

The real-world return process is usually written under \(P\):

\[ dS_t = \mu_P S_t dt + \sigma_t S_t dW_t^P \]

Under risk-neutral pricing, the drift changes so discounted prices become martingales:

\[ dS_t = rS_tdt+\sigma_t S_t dW_t^Q \]

For forwards, the drift is usually removed and we price with:

\[ \frac{dF_t}{F_t} = \sigma_t dW_t^Q \]

The volatility process can also differ under \(P\) and \(Q\). For Heston, the variance mean-reversion level and speed can contain volatility risk premia. A fitted \(\theta\) is therefore the long-run variance level implied by option prices, not necessarily the long-run realized variance we’d estimate from SPX returns.

This is why the project uses the models as pricing and relative-value models rather than direct forecasts of realized future volatility. When a fitted Bates jump intensity is high, the clean interpretation is: the option surface is pricing jump risk strongly. It doesn’t automatically mean the real-world probability of a jump is exactly the fitted \(\lambda\).

Risk Premia and Why Calibration Can Look Strange

Calibrated volatility models often produce parameters that look strange if we read them as historical statistics. That happens because option prices include risk premia.

For example, equity-index options often price downside risk more heavily than the realized frequency of crashes alone might suggest. Investors are willing to pay for crash protection, so the risk-neutral left tail can be heavier than the physical left tail. In model terms, that can show up as:

  • more negative \(\rho\) in Heston,
  • higher \(\xi\) in Heston,
  • negative jump means in Merton/Bates,
  • high jump intensity under \(Q\),
  • steep SVI left-wing slope.

The pricing measure doesn’t need to match historical frequencies exactly. It needs to reproduce the market prices of payoffs. This is why a model can imply a large crash premium even in a calm realized-volatility period.

This distinction also explains why we later validate residuals empirically. If the model’s residual mostly reflects a risk premium that the market intentionally charges, fading it can lose money. A residual becomes useful only if it predicts subsequent repricing or hedged P&L, not simply because it exists.

The first setup cells load the option pairs, Treasury rates, utilities, and plotting style. There’s no methodology to interpret yet. The important point is that the later models all depend on a clean, consistent quote panel. If we fit Heston or Bates to raw, duplicated, illiquid, badly spread quotes, then the model parameters will mostly explain microstructure noise rather than volatility dynamics.

2) Paired Calls, Rates, Forwards, and the Pricing Coordinate System

We start from paired calls and puts because put-call parity gives us the forward. This is important for every model in this project.

For European-style index options, the parity relationship in discounted form is:

\[ C_t(K,T)-P_t(K,T)=D(t,T)\,[F_t(T)-K] \]

Solving for the forward gives:

\[ F_t(T)=K+\frac{C_t(K,T)-P_t(K,T)}{D(t,T)} \]

We do this across many paired strikes for the same date and expiry, then use a robust estimate rather than trusting one strike. The reason is simple: a single quote can be stale or wide. If 150 paired quotes imply almost the same forward but a few bad pairs are outliers, the robust estimate keeps the forward anchored to the liquid part of the chain.

Once we have \(F_t(T)\), the natural moneyness coordinate is:

\[ k=\log\!\left(\frac{K}{F_t(T)}\right) \]

This coordinate is better than raw strike because it puts every expiry on a comparable scale:

  • \(k=0\) means at-the-money forward,
  • \(k<0\) means downside puts / low strikes,
  • \(k>0\) means upside calls / high strikes.

For example, a 5% OTM put and a 5% OTM call are roughly symmetric around \(k=0\), while raw strikes aren’t comparable when the index level changes through time.

Why Forward Moneyness Controls Model Stability

Every smile model in this project becomes cleaner after moving from strike \(K\) to log-forward moneyness \(k\). The forward price already contains the impact of rates, dividends/carry, and maturity. Without that transformation, the same economic strike location would shift mechanically when rates or carry change.

The transformation is:

\[ k=\log(K/F) \]

A few reference points:

  • \(k=0\) means \(K=F\).
  • \(k=-0.10\) means \(K\approx 0.905F\), a roughly 9.5% downside strike.
  • \(k=0.10\) means \(K\approx 1.105F\), a roughly 10.5% upside strike.

Because the logarithm is symmetric in return space, a downside move and upside move become more comparable. A 10% downside strike has:

\[ \log(0.90)\approx -0.105 \]

and a 10% upside strike has:

\[ \log(1.10)\approx 0.095 \]

That is why surfaces are plotted and fitted in \(k\). The shape near \(k=-0.20\) always means “deep downside protection,” regardless of whether SPX is at 3,800 or 5,000.

3) From Paired Quotes to a Long Option Panel

After the forward is inferred, we transform paired call-put rows into a long option table with one row per option quote. This is the format needed for IV solving, Greeks, and model fitting.

For each quote we now have a pricing identity:

\[ \text{observed price} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \sigma_{imp} \]

The implied volatility is the value of \(\sigma\) that solves:

\[ V^{B76}(F,K,T,D,\sigma)=V^{mkt} \]

where \(V^{B76}\) is the Black-76 price and \(V^{mkt}\) is the option mid, bid, or ask. We don’t re-derive the Black-76 solver here because that was already done in the earlier option project. What matters here is how the solved IV becomes the modeling target.

The full project repeatedly moves between three spaces:

Space Object Why we use it
Price space \(V^{mkt}\) and \(V^{model}\) Needed for real P&L, bid-ask costs, and Monte Carlo pricing models
Implied-vol space \(\sigma_{imp}\) Makes model errors comparable across strikes and maturities
Total-variance space \(w(k,T)=\sigma_{imp}^2(k,T)T\) Usually smoother and safer for surface parameterizations

That last column drives a lot of the project. SVI and SSVI fit total variance. SABR produces implied volatility. Merton, Heston, and Bates naturally produce prices, then we invert those prices back into IV for diagnostics.

Price Error, IV Error, and Total-Variance Error

We use three error scales because each one answers a different question.

A price error is:

\[ e_i^V=V_i^{model}-V_i^{mkt} \]

This is closest to actual tradable money. If the model is $2 above the market mid, that can look like a cheap option. But price errors are hard to compare across strikes. A $2 error on a $300 option is small. A $2 error on a $1 option is huge.

An implied-vol error is:

\[ e_i^\sigma=\sigma_i^{model}-\sigma_i^{mkt} \]

This makes errors more comparable across strikes and maturities. A 50 vol-bp error means something interpretable. But IV error can exaggerate very low-vega regions because tiny price changes can imply large IV changes.

A total-variance error is:

\[ e_i^w=w_i^{model}-w_i^{mkt} \]

with:

\[ w_i=\sigma_i^2T_i \]

Total variance is useful for surface parameterizations because variance accumulates with time. If the one-month vol is \(20\%\), the total variance is roughly:

\[ 0.20^2 \times \frac{1}{12}=0.0033 \]

If the one-year vol is \(20\%\), the total variance is:

\[ 0.20^2 \times 1=0.04 \]

The volatility number is the same, but the variance budget is very different. SVI and SSVI work in this accumulated-variance space because it behaves more smoothly across maturities.

Error Translation Through Vega

The link between price error and IV error is approximately vega:

\[ e_i^V \approx \mathcal{V}_i e_i^\sigma \]

so:

\[ e_i^\sigma \approx \frac{e_i^V}{\mathcal{V}_i} \]

This is why model comparison in both price and IV space is needed. A model can have a small price error on a low-vega option but a large IV error. It can also have a large dollar error on a high-vega option but a small IV error.

For example, a $1 price error on an option with vega \(500\) is:

\[ \frac{1}{500}=0.002 \]

or about 20 vol basis points. The same $1 error on an option with vega \(20\) is:

\[ \frac{1}{20}=0.05 \]

or 5 vol points. Those two errors have completely different meaning.

This is also why the project never treats deep wings casually. Deep OTM options can have low vega, wide spreads, and jump-sensitive prices. They are exactly where stochastic models are interesting, but also where diagnostics have to be strict.

The long quote preview confirms that calls and puts are stacked separately at the same strike and expiry. Very deep OTM options can have tiny prices and wide relative spreads, so a valid row in the table isn’t automatically a good modeling quote. We still need filtering, OTM selection, vega checks, and bid-ask-aware weights.

The IV solving step is large: more than 4.0 million rows are processed, with about 3.99 million valid mid IV quotes. The engine is numba, and the solve takes about 50.8 seconds in the executed run. That is a useful engineering result because stochastic-volatility work becomes impossible if the data preparation layer is already too slow.

4) Greeks, Data Quality, and the Model-Ready Quote Set

After IV solving, we compute Greeks because they enter two later tasks:

  1. uncertainty scaling, because a price error translates into an IV error through vega,
  2. delta-hedged backtesting, because the trading experiment needs hedge ratios.

The basic local approximation is:

\[ dV \approx \mathcal{V}\,d\sigma \]

where \(\mathcal{V}\) is vega. Rearranging gives the rough IV uncertainty implied by a price uncertainty:

\[ d\sigma \approx \frac{dV}{\mathcal{V}} \]

This is why a $0.50 bid-ask half-spread isn’t equally meaningful everywhere. If vega is very high, that half-spread corresponds to a small IV uncertainty. If vega is almost zero, the same half-spread can mean the implied volatility is poorly pinned down.

A simple example makes this clear. If an option has vega \(200\) and the half-spread is \(0.50\), the spread-implied IV uncertainty is about \(0.0025\), or 25 volatility basis points:

\[ \frac{0.50}{200}=0.0025 \]

If another option has vega \(5\) with the same half-spread, the implied IV uncertainty becomes \(0.10\), which is 10 vol points. The second quote is much less useful for calibration even if the dollar spread looks the same.

t0 = tic()
quote_panel = compute_greeks_numpy(q_iv, iv_col="iv_mid")
quote_panel["relative_spread"] = pd.to_numeric(quote_panel["relative_spread"], errors="coerce")
quote_panel["spread"] = pd.to_numeric(quote_panel["ask"], errors="coerce") - pd.to_numeric(quote_panel["bid"], errors="coerce")
quote_panel["total_var"] = quote_panel["iv_mid"] ** 2 * quote_panel["tau"]
quote_panel["total_variance"] = quote_panel["total_var"]


def make_contract_key(df):
    expiry_key = pd.to_datetime(df["expiry"]).dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    strike_key = df["strike"].astype(float).map(lambda x: f"{x:.8g}")
    return df["option_type"].astype(str) + "_" + expiry_key + "_" + strike_key


quote_panel["contract_key"] = make_contract_key(quote_panel)
quote_panel["contract_id"] = quote_panel["contract_key"]
toc("compute greeks", t0, len(quote_panel))

5) OTM Selection, Quote Support, and Observation Uncertainty

We now build the surface-ready panel. The main filters are:

  • DTE between about 14 and 150 days for calibration,
  • log-moneyness window around \(|k|\le 0.32\),
  • minimum vega,
  • maximum relative spread,
  • one OTM option leg per strike.

The OTM rule is important. Calls and puts with the same strike and expiry contain almost the same volatility information once the forward and discount factor are known. Keeping both sides can double-count strikes and overweight some parts of the surface. We keep the out-of-the-money side because it’s usually more liquid in volatility terms and more directly reflects the part of the smile traders care about.

Mathematically, after parity adjustment, a call and put at the same \(K,T\) imply the same volatility if markets are frictionless. In real data they can disagree because of bid-ask, stale quotes, and exercise/microstructure details. The OTM selection is a practical compromise:

\[ \text{one strike} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{one cleaner volatility observation} \]

The model panel is slightly looser than the main calibration panel because stochastic models like Merton, Heston, and Bates need tail points to identify jumps and stochastic-volatility skew. If we make the quote set too strict, the tails disappear and those models become underidentified.

Why OTM Quotes Are the Cleanest Volatility Quotes

For a given strike and expiry, call and put prices are tied by parity:

\[ C-P=D(F-K) \]

If parity holds exactly, the implied volatility from the call and the put must match. If they don’t match, the difference usually comes from market friction rather than a new volatility signal. It is often bid-ask noise, stale quotes, or parity friction.

OTM options are usually preferred for implied-volatility surfaces because:

  • OTM options are more actively quoted for volatility exposure,
  • ITM options have large intrinsic value that can dominate the option premium,
  • small errors in parity or forwards can distort ITM implied vol more visibly,
  • the OTM side lines up with how traders quote downside puts and upside calls.

So for \(K<F\), the put is OTM and is usually kept. For \(K>F\), the call is OTM and is usually kept. Around ATM, either side can be used, but the implementation keeps one clean quote per strike.

This matters even more for stochastic models. If we double-count call and put at every strike, the optimization can overweight the center and underweight the actual tail information. A model like Bates then calibrates to duplicated structure rather than to a balanced view of the surface.

q_surface = surface_ready_quotes(
    quote_panel,
    min_iv=0.03,
    max_iv=2.50,
    min_tau=7.0 / ann_days,
    max_tau=180.0 / ann_days,
)
q_surface["total_var"] = q_surface["total_variance"]
q_surface["log_moneyness"] = q_surface["k"]
min_dte, max_dte, min_vega, max_rel_spread = 14.0, 150.0, 8.0, 0.45
max_abs_k, min_quotes_per_expiry, min_expiries_per_date = 0.32, 8, 5
def make_otm_quotes(q, min_vega_use=None, max_rel_spread_use=None, min_quotes_use=None):
    x = q.copy()
    rows = []
    vega_floor = min_vega if min_vega_use is None else float(min_vega_use)
    spread_cap = max_rel_spread if max_rel_spread_use is None else float(max_rel_spread_use)
    strike_floor = min_quotes_per_expiry if min_quotes_use is None else int(min_quotes_use)

    def cut(name, mask):
        nonlocal x
        before = len(x)
        x = x.loc[mask].copy()
        rows.append({"step": name, "rows": len(x), "removed": before - len(x)})

    rows.append({"step": "surface ready", "rows": len(x), "removed": 0})
    cut("positive quotes", (x["bid"] > 0) & (x["ask"] >= x["bid"]) & (x["mid"] > 0))
    cut("valid iv inputs", x["iv_ok"].fillna(False) & np.isfinite(x["forward"]) & np.isfinite(x["discount_factor"]) & (x["forward"] > 0) & (x["discount_factor"] > 0))
    cut("dte window", x["dte_days"].between(min_dte, max_dte))
    cut("k window", x["k"].between(-max_abs_k, max_abs_k))
    cut("vega and spread", (np.abs(x["vega"]) >= vega_floor) & x["relative_spread"].between(0.0, spread_cap))

    atm = 0.0125
    x["otm_type"] = np.where(x["k"] < -atm, "put", np.where(x["k"] > atm, "call", "either"))
    med_spread = float(np.nanmedian(x["relative_spread"])) if x["relative_spread"].notna().any() else 0.25
    x["q_score"] = x["relative_spread"].fillna(med_spread) + 0.02 * x["k"].abs()
    x["type_penalty"] = np.where((x["otm_type"] == "either") | (x["option_type"] == x["otm_type"]), 0.0, 1.0)
    before = len(x)
    x = x.sort_values(["date", "expiry", "strike", "type_penalty", "q_score"]).drop_duplicates(["date", "expiry", "strike"], keep="first").copy()
    rows.append({"step": "one otm leg per strike", "rows": len(x), "removed": before - len(x)})

    n = x.groupby(["date", "expiry"]).size().rename("n")
    keep = n[n >= strike_floor].index
    before = len(x)
    x = x.loc[x.set_index(["date", "expiry"]).index.isin(keep)].copy()
    rows.append({"step": "enough strikes", "rows": len(x), "removed": before - len(x)})

    m = x.groupby("date")["expiry"].nunique().rename("m")
    keep_dates = m[m >= min_expiries_per_date].index
    before = len(x)
    x = x[x["date"].isin(keep_dates)].copy()
    rows.append({"step": "enough expiries", "rows": len(x), "removed": before - len(x)})

    x = x.sort_values(["date", "expiry", "strike"]).reset_index(drop=True)
    x["quote_id"] = np.arange(len(x), dtype=int)
    x["contract_id"] = x["option_type"].astype(str) + "_" + pd.to_datetime(x["expiry"]).dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") + "_" + x["strike"].round(6).astype(str)
    return x, pd.DataFrame(rows)
min_vega_model, max_rel_spread_model, n_model_dates = 2.0, 0.65, 6
calibration_panel, rejection_summary = make_otm_quotes(q_surface)
model_panel, model_rejection_summary = make_otm_quotes(q_surface, min_vega_use=min_vega_model, max_rel_spread_use=max_rel_spread_model, min_quotes_use=7)
calibration_panel["contract_key"] = make_contract_key(calibration_panel)
model_panel["contract_key"] = make_contract_key(model_panel)
calibration_panel["contract_id"] = calibration_panel["contract_key"]
model_panel["contract_id"] = model_panel["contract_key"]
support0 = quote_support_by_date(calibration_panel, k_col="k", tau_col="tau")
by_date = calibration_panel.groupby("date").agg(
    quotes=("quote_id", "size"),
    expiries=("expiry", "nunique"),
    median_relative_spread=("relative_spread", "median"),
    median_iv=("iv_mid", "median"),

    wing_quotes=("k", lambda z: int(np.sum(np.abs(z) >= 0.15))),
).reset_index()
model_by_date = model_panel.groupby("date").agg(
    model_quotes=("quote_id", "size"),
    model_expiries=("expiry", "nunique"),
    model_k_min=("k", "min"),

    model_left_tail=("k", lambda z: int(np.sum(z <= -0.14))),
    model_right_tail=("k", lambda z: int(np.sum(z >= 0.10))),

surface_support_by_date = support0.merge(by_date, on="date", how="left", suffixes=("", "_detail"))
surface_support_by_date = surface_support_by_date.merge(model_by_date, on="date", how="left")

surface_support_by_date["model_k_width"] = surface_support_by_date["model_k_max"] - surface_support_by_date["model_k_min"]
surface_support_by_date["score"] = (
    surface_support_by_date["quotes"].fillna(0)
    + 25.0 * surface_support_by_date["expiries"].fillna(0)
    + 1.5 * surface_support_by_date["near_atm_quotes"].fillna(0)
    + surface_support_by_date["wing_quotes"].fillna(0)
    + 0.6 * surface_support_by_date["model_tail_count"].fillna(0)
    + 150.0 * surface_support_by_date["model_k_width"].fillna(0)
    + 120.0 * surface_support_by_date["k_width"].fillna(0)
    - 80.0 * surface_support_by_date["median_relative_spread"].fillna(0.50)
)
good_dates = surface_support_by_date[
    (surface_support_by_date["quotes"] >= 120)
    & (surface_support_by_date["expiries"] >= min_expiries_per_date)
    & (surface_support_by_date["near_atm_quotes"] >= 18)
].copy()
if good_dates.empty:
    good_dates = surface_support_by_date.sort_values("score", ascending=False).head(20).copy()
tail_dates = good_dates[
    (good_dates["model_left_tail"].fillna(0) >= 8)
    & (good_dates["model_tail_count"].fillna(0) >= 16)
].copy()
main_pool = tail_dates if not tail_dates.empty else good_dates
recent_cut = main_pool["date"].quantile(0.65)
main_date = pd.Timestamp(main_pool[main_pool["date"] >= recent_cut].sort_values("score", ascending=False).iloc[0]["date"]).normalize()
date_panel_dates = good_dates.sort_values("score", ascending=False).head(n_model_dates)["date"].sort_values().to_numpy()
q0 = calibration_panel[calibration_panel["date"].eq(main_date)].copy()
q_model0 = model_panel[model_panel["date"].eq(main_date)].copy()
date_panel = calibration_panel[calibration_panel["date"].isin(date_panel_dates)].copy()
date_model_panel = model_panel[model_panel["date"].isin(date_panel_dates)].copy()

The quote-support plot by expiry shows dense coverage across several maturities, not only one isolated expiry. The scatter of IV by \(k\) and maturity has the familiar SPX structure: downside puts have much higher implied vol than ATM and upside calls. The front part of the surface is also more elevated and more curved. This is the empirical shape the models have to explain.

The heatmap of quote count by maturity and \(k\) bucket shows where the surface is actually observed. The middle-left region is the most populated: near-ATM to moderately downside strikes and short-to-medium maturities. The far right wing and far left wing are thinner. That means a model can look impressive visually while still being mostly determined by the center of the surface. Tail diagnostics later are needed because the tails don’t have the same quote density as the center.

Support Density and Calibration Trust

The support plots tell us which parts of the fitted surface deserve trust.

A dense area of the surface means many liquid quotes are telling the model the same local story. A sparse area means the model is extrapolating more. In a dense region, a residual is more likely to be meaningful. In a sparse wing, a residual can be an artifact of interpolation, quote noise, or model assumptions.

This is why the later fair-value logic includes model disagreement and quote uncertainty. The surface can always return a number, even where data support is weak. A serious model has to know when that number is fragile.

On the main SPX date, the dense region is short-to-medium maturity and near-ATM to moderate downside. That is the strongest calibration region. The extreme right wing and very far downside wing are thinner, so tail interpretations need more caution.

Bid-Ask-Aware Uncertainty

We assign every quote an uncertainty scale. This is a core design choice because calibration is an estimation problem with noisy observations.

For implied volatility we combine two uncertainty estimates:

\[ \epsilon_{\sigma,\text{direct}}=\frac{\sigma_{ask}-\sigma_{bid}}{2} \]

and:

\[ \epsilon_{\sigma,\text{price}}=\frac{\text{half-spread}}{\mathcal{V}} \]

Then we use a conservative value:

\[ \epsilon_\sigma=\max(\epsilon_{\sigma,\text{direct}},\epsilon_{\sigma,\text{price}}) \]

The total-variance uncertainty follows from:

\[ w=\sigma^2T \]

A first-order derivative gives:

\[ dw=2\sigma T\,d\sigma \]

so the total-variance scale is:

\[ \epsilon_w \approx 2\sigma_{imp}T\epsilon_\sigma \]

For price-space models, the relevant calibration scale is based on price uncertainty:

\[ \epsilon_V=\max(\text{half-spread}, \mathcal{V}\epsilon_\sigma) \]

This way, a model isn’t punished heavily for missing a quote by less than the market’s own uncertainty, and it is punished more when it misses a tight, liquid quote.

Weighted Least Squares as a Statistical Model

The calibration objective can be read as a weighted Gaussian measurement model. Suppose the observed target \(y_i\) is the true model value plus quote noise:

\[ y_i=f(x_i;\theta)+\varepsilon_i \]

with:

\[ \varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\epsilon_i^2) \]

Then the negative log-likelihood is proportional to:

\[ \sum_i \left(\frac{f(x_i;\theta)-y_i}{\epsilon_i}\right)^2 \]

This is exactly the weighted residual logic used throughout the project. A quote with large \(\epsilon_i\) has a wider noise distribution, so a larger miss is statistically less surprising. A tight quote has a small \(\epsilon_i\), so even a small miss is meaningful.

When we add quote weights \(\omega_i\), the objective becomes:

\[ \sum_i \omega_i\left(\frac{f(x_i;\theta)-y_i}{\epsilon_i}\right)^2 \]

The weight can also rebalance maturity buckets or de-emphasize poor quote regions. So the calibration objective is doing two things at once:

  1. measuring residuals in uncertainty units,
  2. controlling which regions of the surface have influence.

This is why calibration means estimating a model under noisy observations, not simply drawing a smooth curve.

Robust Loss and Parameter Bounds

Several calibrations use bounded least squares and robust losses. The bounded part means parameters are constrained to plausible ranges:

\[ \theta_{min}\le \theta \le \theta_{max} \]

This matters because unconstrained optimizers can find mathematically possible but economically useless fits. For example:

  • \(\rho\) outside \([-1,1]\) is impossible as a correlation.
  • negative vol-of-vol has no meaning.
  • negative jump volatility has no meaning.
  • extremely large jump intensity can compensate for a tiny jump size in unstable ways.

The robust loss, such as a soft-\(L_1\) style loss, reduces the influence of extreme residuals. In ordinary least squares, one extreme quote can dominate because squared errors grow very fast:

\[ L(r)=r^2 \]

A robust loss behaves quadratically near zero but grows more slowly for large residuals. That is useful for option chains because some quotes are simply bad or stale even after cleaning.

The bound-warning diagnostics later tell us whether the optimizer is pushing against the edges of the parameter box. If a parameter is at a bound, the fit may be saying: the model wants something more extreme than we allowed. That is a warning about misspecification or weak identification.


def add_quote_sigma(q):
    x = q.copy()
    x["half_spread"] = 0.5 * (pd.to_numeric(x["ask"], errors="coerce") - pd.to_numeric(x["bid"], errors="coerce")).clip(lower=0.0)
    vega = np.abs(pd.to_numeric(x["vega"], errors="coerce"))
    x["iv_width"] = (pd.to_numeric(x["iv_ask"], errors="coerce") - pd.to_numeric(x["iv_bid"], errors="coerce")).where(lambda s: np.isfinite(s) & (s > 0))
    x["sigma_iv_direct"] = 0.5 * x["iv_width"]
    x["sigma_iv_px"] = x["half_spread"] / vega.replace(0, np.nan)
    eps_iv = pd.concat([x["sigma_iv_direct"], x["sigma_iv_px"]], axis=1).max(axis=1)
    med = float(np.nanmedian(eps_iv)) if np.isfinite(eps_iv).any() else 0.020
    x["eps_iv"] = eps_iv.fillna(med).clip(lower=0.0025, upper=0.40)
    x["total_var"] = x["iv_mid"] ** 2 * x["tau"]
    x["eps_w"] = (2.0 * x["iv_mid"].abs() * x["tau"] * x["eps_iv"]).clip(lower=1e-5)
    x["calib_scale_px"] = np.maximum(x["half_spread"], 0.25 * vega * x["eps_iv"]).clip(lower=0.02)
    x["eps_px"] = np.maximum(x["half_spread"], vega * x["eps_iv"]).clip(lower=0.02)
    x["expected_exit_half_spread"] = x.groupby(["date", "expiry"])["half_spread"].transform("median").fillna(x["half_spread"].median())
    x["trade_cost_px"] = x["half_spread"] + 0.5 * x["expected_exit_half_spread"]

    spread = x["relative_spread"].replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    spread_med = float(np.nanmedian(spread[(spread > 0) & np.isfinite(spread)])) if spread.notna().any() else 0.10
    spread = spread.fillna(spread_med).clip(lower=0.003, upper=1.0)
    w_spread = 1.0 / (spread.to_numpy(dtype=float) ** 2 + 0.03 ** 2)
    w_spread = w_spread / max(float(np.nanmedian(w_spread)), 1e-12)

    vega_med = float(np.nanmedian(vega[(vega > 0) & np.isfinite(vega)])) if np.isfinite(vega).any() else 1.0
    w_vega = np.clip((vega.to_numpy(dtype=float) / max(vega_med, 1e-12)) ** 0.40, 0.20, 3.0)
    eps = x["eps_iv"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    eps_med = float(np.nanmedian(eps[np.isfinite(eps) & (eps > 0)])) if np.isfinite(eps).any() else 0.02
    w_eps = np.clip(eps / max(eps_med, 1e-12), 0.45, 4.0) ** -0.70
    w_k = np.exp(-np.maximum(np.abs(x["k"].to_numpy(dtype=float)) - 0.12, 0.0) / 0.35)
    n_exp = x.groupby(["date", "expiry"])["quote_id"].transform("count").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    w_tau = 1.0 / np.sqrt(np.maximum(n_exp, 1.0))
    w_tau = w_tau / max(float(np.nanmedian(w_tau)), 1e-12)
    wt = w_spread * w_vega * w_eps * w_k * w_tau
    wt = wt / max(float(np.nanmedian(wt[np.isfinite(wt)])), 1e-12)
    x["w_spread"] = w_spread
    x["w_vega"] = w_vega
    x["w_eps"] = w_eps
    x["w_k"] = w_k
    x["w_tau"] = w_tau
    x["weight"] = np.clip(wt, 0.05, 20.0)
    return x
calibration_panel = add_quote_sigma(calibration_panel)
model_panel = add_quote_sigma(model_panel)
q0 = calibration_panel[calibration_panel["date"].eq(main_date)].copy()
q_model0 = model_panel[model_panel["date"].eq(main_date)].copy()
date_panel = calibration_panel[calibration_panel["date"].isin(date_panel_dates)].copy()
date_model_panel = model_panel[model_panel["date"].isin(date_panel_dates)].copy()
uncertainty_by_maturity = q0.assign(dte_bucket=pd.cut(q0["dte_days"], bins=[0, 21, 45, 75, 110, 180])).groupby("dte_bucket", observed=False).agg(
    quotes=("quote_id", "size"),

The maturity uncertainty table shows a very clean pattern. Median IV uncertainty is clipped at 0.0025 across buckets, while median price uncertainty rises with maturity: about 0.44 for the shortest bucket, then 0.79, 1.31, 1.74, and 1.92 for longer maturities. That is economically sensible because longer-dated options have more dollar value and higher vega, so price-scale uncertainty naturally grows even if IV uncertainty stays tight.

The weight plots also show the intended behavior. Very wide relative spreads receive lower weights, while liquid high-vega quotes receive higher weights. This is exactly what we want: the models should listen most to quotes where the market price is informative.

6) Model Targets: What Each Model Is Trying to Explain

Before fitting anything, we define the target space for each model:

Model Main fitted object Why this target fits the model
SVI total variance \(w(k,T)\) SVI is a smile parameterization in total variance
SSVI total variance \(w(k,T)\) SSVI imposes a global surface structure around ATM total variance
SABR implied volatility \(\sigma_{imp}\) Hagan’s approximation directly gives implied vol
Merton option price \(V\) jump-diffusion prices are generated from a distribution
Heston simulated option price \(V\) stochastic variance defines a risk-neutral future distribution
Bates simulated option price \(V\) stochastic variance plus jumps defines a richer distribution

This separation is essential. A model that minimizes IV error and a model that minimizes price error aren’t solving exactly the same problem. IV error treats a one-vol-point miss similarly across the surface. Price error matters more where the option has high dollar sensitivity. Price-space models are closer to tradable P&L, but they are slower and can be noisier because the pricing engine has to simulate or integrate a distribution.

We use both spaces later. Fit quality in IV terms tells us how well a model explains the surface shape. Fit quality in price terms tells us how much money the miss might matter in actual option prices.

Calibration as an Inverse Problem

Every model calibration here is an inverse problem. The forward problem is:

\[ \theta \rightarrow V^{model}(\theta) \]

Given parameters \(\theta\), we can compute model prices or implied vols. Calibration reverses this:

\[ V^{mkt} \rightarrow \hat{\theta} \]

This inverse problem is often ill-conditioned. Small quote changes can move parameters a lot, especially when parameters affect similar parts of the surface. For example:

  • in Heston, more negative \(\rho\) and higher \(\xi\) can both steepen the left skew,
  • in Bates, negative jumps and stochastic variance can both raise OTM put prices,
  • in SABR, \(\rho\) and \(\nu\) can trade off between skew and curvature,
  • in SVI, \(b\), \(\rho\), \(m\), and \(\sigma\) can combine to produce similar-looking smiles.

So the diagnostic tables are part of the modeling, not decoration. Success flags, bound warnings, runtime, residual heatmaps, Monte Carlo standard error, and holdout error are all ways of checking whether the inverse problem produced a stable result.

Parameter Identification and Economic Plausibility

Identification means whether the data can distinguish one parameter effect from another. This is a central issue in volatility modeling.

For SVI, identification is usually acceptable because each parameter has a geometric role and we have many strike observations per expiry. But even there, parameters can trade off. A shift in \(m\) and a change in \(\rho\) can both affect where the smile is steepest.

For Heston, identification is harder. The option surface may say “I need a steep left wing,” and the model can create that through several combinations:

\[ \rho \downarrow,\quad \xi \uparrow,\quad \theta \uparrow,\quad v_0 \downarrow \]

These changes don’t have identical effects, but they overlap enough that a small quote panel can’t always separate them cleanly. Bates adds even more overlap because jumps can also steepen tails:

\[ \lambda \uparrow,\quad \mu_J \downarrow,\quad \sigma_J \uparrow \]

A parameter set is more believable when it fits well, avoids bounds, has reasonable standard errors/noise, and remains stable across nearby dates. This project doesn’t estimate full parameter uncertainty distributions, but it does record warning flags and MC standard errors so we don’t overstate precision.

7) SVI: Slice-Level Smile Modeling in Total Variance

The first model family is SVI, which stands for stochastic volatility inspired. Despite the name, in this implementation SVI is a static smile parameterization. For each expiry, it fits a curve in log-moneyness \(k\):

\[ w(k)=a+b\left(\rho(k-m)+\sqrt{(k-m)^2+\sigma^2}\right) \]

where \(w(k)=\sigma_{imp}^2(k,T)T\) is total implied variance for a fixed maturity. Each parameter has a visible shape role:

  • \(a\) lifts the whole curve up or down.
  • \(b\) controls the overall slope/wing steepness.
  • \(\rho\) controls skew direction. For SPX, \(\rho\) is usually negative because downside puts are expensive.
  • \(m\) shifts the center of the smile left or right in moneyness.
  • \(\sigma\) controls the smoothness/curvature around the smile center.

The square-root term is the main reason SVI is useful. It behaves smoothly near the center but becomes close to linear in the wings. That lets the curve fit a U-shaped smile or skew without exploding as badly as a high-order polynomial.

For a fixed expiry, the market gives us observations:

\[ (k_i,w_i), \quad i=1,\ldots,n \]

and we estimate parameters \(\theta=(a,b,\rho,m,\sigma)\) by minimizing a weighted residual objective:

\[ \min_\theta \sum_{i=1}^{n}\omega_i\left(\frac{w_{SVI}(k_i;\theta)-w_i}{\epsilon_{w,i}}\right)^2 \]

The term \(\epsilon_{w,i}\) is the total-variance uncertainty from bid-ask and vega. So the residual is measured in “number of quote-uncertainty units,” not raw variance units.

If a quote is very precise, missing it matters. If a quote is noisy, missing it slightly doesn’t mean the model is bad.

SVI Wing Slopes and Why the Formula Works

SVI is especially useful because the left and right wings become almost linear for large \(|k-m|\). For large positive \(x=k-m\):

\[ \sqrt{x^2+\sigma^2}\approx |x| \]

so on the right wing:

\[ w(k)\approx a+b(\rho x+x)=a+b(1+\rho)x \]

and on the left wing, where \(x<0\):

\[ w(k)\approx a+b(\rho x-x)=a+b(\rho-1)x \]

Because \(x\) is negative on the left, a negative value of \((\rho-1)x\) raises total variance. If \(\rho<0\), the left wing becomes steeper than the right wing. That is the equity-index skew.

The wing slope intuition is:

\[ \text{right wing slope}\approx b(1+\rho) \]

\[ \text{left wing slope}\approx b(\rho-1) \]

A more negative \(\rho\) lowers the right wing slope and steepens the left wing. That is why \(\rho\) is one of the most economically meaningful SVI parameters for SPX.

The parameter \(\sigma\) controls how sharp the transition is around \(m\). If \(\sigma\) is small, the curve can bend more sharply near the center. If it is large, the curve is smoother and flatter around the minimum.

So SVI has a clear geometry: level, wing steepness, skew direction, center shift, and curvature width.

Why SVI Is a Strong Fair-Value Core

SVI has three practical strengths that make it a natural fair-value core.

First, it is flexible enough to fit the smile shape in each expiry without needing too many parameters. Five parameters per expiry is a good compromise: more flexible than a quadratic curve, less fragile than a high-order polynomial.

Second, it is fast. Even fitting 29 expiries and thousands of quotes is feasible. That matters because the validation section fits many daily surfaces.

Third, it has interpretable residuals. If SVI misses a point, that miss is measured relative to a local smooth smile. This is close to how option traders think: they build a smooth volatility curve and look for quotes that sit above or below it.

The limitation is that SVI residuals can reflect the model’s own flexibility. A flexible model can bend around noise. That is why SVI is combined with holdout scoring, model disagreement, and validation rather than being treated as a final arbitrage signal by itself.

def svi_w_demo(k, a, b, rho, m, sigma):
    return a + b * (rho * (k - m) + np.sqrt((k - m) ** 2 + sigma ** 2))


k_line = np.linspace(-0.35, 0.35, 240)
tau_demo = 60.0 / ann_days
p_demo = [
    (0.010, 0.030, -0.60, 0.000, 0.120, "balanced skew"),
    (0.008, 0.045, -0.85, -0.030, 0.080, "strong downside wing"),
    (0.012, 0.025, 0.20, 0.020, 0.160, "gentler curvature"),
]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 4.4))
for a, b, rho, m, sigma, label in p_demo:
    ax.plot(k_line, np.sqrt(np.maximum(svi_w_demo(k_line, a, b, rho, m, sigma), 1e-8) / tau_demo), lw=2.0, label=label)
ax.set_title("raw svi total-variance smiles")
ax.set_xlabel("k")
ax.set_ylabel("implied volatility")

The demo plot shows how SVI parameters change the smile. The strong downside-wing curve has a much steeper left wing, which is the SPX crash-protection shape. The balanced version has a smoother skew, and the gentler curvature version is flatter around ATM.

A useful way to read SVI is to think of it as a local smile language. It doesn’t tell us why volatility moves. It tells us how to summarize one expiry’s smile using five numbers. That is already valuable because a raw expiry can have 100 to 200 quotes. Compressing those quotes into five interpretable parameters gives us a much more manageable object for diagnostics.

SVI Fitting Details

For every expiry we:

  1. sort quotes by \(k\),
  2. fit total variance \(w(k)\),
  3. use multiple starting points to avoid a weak local minimum,
  4. include previous expiry parameters as a warm start when possible,
  5. record weighted IV RMSE, median absolute IV error, P90 absolute IV error, and parameter-bound warnings.

The warm-start idea matters because adjacent expiries usually have related smile shapes. If the 45-day smile and the 50-day smile are wildly different, that’s often a data issue or optimization issue rather than true market structure. Reusing the previous slice as a candidate start helps stabilize the term structure of parameters.

SVI and Static Arbitrage Intuition

Option surfaces have basic no-arbitrage requirements. We don’t re-build the full no-arbitrage machinery here, but it helps to understand what can go wrong.

For a fixed maturity, call prices must be decreasing and convex in strike:

\[ \frac{\partial C}{\partial K}\le 0 \]

\[ \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial K^2}\ge 0 \]

The second condition is butterfly arbitrage: if the call price curve isn’t convex, a butterfly spread can have negative cost and nonnegative payoff.

Across maturities, total variance should usually be nondecreasing in maturity for the same moneyness coordinate:

\[ \frac{\partial w(k,T)}{\partial T}\ge 0 \]

This is linked to calendar-spread arbitrage. Longer maturity options shouldn’t be cheaper in a way that creates free time value.

Raw SVI slice fitting doesn’t automatically enforce all cross-maturity conditions. It can fit each expiry beautifully and still create an irregular term structure. That is why SSVI exists in the next section. The project keeps both models because they solve different problems: SVI gives precise local fit, while SSVI adds surface-level discipline.

Why We Still Use Raw SVI Despite Arbitrage Concerns

Raw slice SVI can create cross-maturity irregularities, but it remains extremely useful because this project’s trading signal is local and short-horizon. We aren’t using raw SVI to price long-dated exotic books. We are using it to estimate a fair value for listed options on a dense surface date.

That matters because the model’s job determines the required strictness. For exotic pricing, an arbitrage-free global surface is crucial. For daily residual ranking, local fit and holdout validation can be more important.

The project still protects itself in three ways:

  1. SSVI is fitted as a disciplined global cross-check.
  2. Residuals are uncertainty-adjusted with model disagreement.
  3. Historical validation checks whether residuals work out of sample.

So raw SVI is used where it is strongest, and its weaknesses are controlled by diagnostics rather than ignored.

Local Flexibility and Overfitting Risk

SVI’s flexibility is useful, but it creates overfitting risk. If a slice has a few noisy quotes, SVI might bend toward them. That can create a false residual nearby or hide a true residual by absorbing it into the fitted curve.

The project controls this through:

  • quote weights,
  • multiple starting values,
  • parameter-bound checks,
  • residual plots,
  • SSVI/SABR comparison,
  • holdout scoring,
  • historical validation.

This sequence is important. We don’t trust SVI because it has a pretty fit. We trust it conditionally because it passes several diagnostic layers and then gets tested out of sample.

This is also why raw calibration RMSE isn’t enough. A model with very low in-sample error can be worse for trading if it overfits noise. The holdout and validation sections are the protection against that.

@njit
def svi_w(k, a, b, rho, m, sigma):
    out = np.empty(k.size, dtype=np.float64)
    for i in range(k.size):
        x = k[i] - m
        out[i] = a + b * (rho * x + math.sqrt(x * x + sigma * sigma))
    return out


@njit
def svi_iv(k, tau, a, b, rho, m, sigma):
    w = svi_w(k, a, b, rho, m, sigma)
    out = np.empty(k.size, dtype=np.float64)
    for i in range(k.size):
        out[i] = math.sqrt(max(w[i], 1e-12) / max(tau[i], 1e-12))
    return out


t0 = tic()
_ = svi_w(np.array([0.0, 0.1]), 0.01, 0.04, -0.4, 0.0, 0.12)
svi_compile_time = toc("compile svi", t0, 2)
def wrmse(x, wt):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    wt = np.asarray(wt, dtype=float)
    ok = np.isfinite(x) & np.isfinite(wt) & (wt > 0)
    if ok.sum() == 0:
        return np.nan
    return float(np.sqrt(np.average(x[ok] ** 2, weights=wt[ok])))


def near_bound(p, lo, hi, tol=2e-3):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    lo = np.asarray(lo, dtype=float)
    hi = np.asarray(hi, dtype=float)
    scale = np.maximum(hi - lo, 1e-12)
    return bool(np.any((p - lo) / scale < tol) or np.any((hi - p) / scale < tol))
def svi_starts(q, p_prev=None):
    k = q["k"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    w = q["total_var"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    iv = q["iv_mid"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    i0 = int(np.nanargmin(np.abs(k)))
    w0 = float(np.clip(w[i0], 1e-5, 2.0))
    slope = float(np.polyfit(k, w, 1)[0]) if len(q) >= 5 else 0.0
    starts = [
        np.array([0.35 * w0, max(0.02, 1.2 * abs(slope)), -0.50, 0.0, 0.10]),
        np.array([0.20 * w0, max(0.03, 0.8 * np.nanmedian(iv) ** 2), -0.75, float(k[i0]), 0.08]),
        np.array([0.55 * w0, max(0.01, 0.5 * abs(slope) + 0.015), -0.25, float(np.nanmedian(k)), 0.18]),
    ]
    if p_prev is not None and np.all(np.isfinite(p_prev)):
        starts.insert(0, np.asarray(p_prev, dtype=float))
    return starts


def fit_svi_slice(q, p_prev=None):
    z = q.sort_values("k").copy()
    k = z["k"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    y = z["total_var"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    eps = z["eps_w"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    eps_med = float(np.nanmedian(eps[np.isfinite(eps) & (eps > 0)])) if np.isfinite(eps).any() else 1e-4
    eps = np.clip(eps, max(1e-5, 0.25 * eps_med), 0.25)
    root_wt = np.sqrt(z["weight"].to_numpy(dtype=float))
    lo = np.array([-0.20, 1e-5, -0.999, -0.80, 1e-4])
    hi = np.array([2.00, 5.00, 0.999, 0.80, 2.00])

    def err(p):
        w = np.asarray(svi_w(k, p[0], p[1], p[2], p[3], p[4]), dtype=float)
        r = root_wt * (w - y) / eps
        r = np.where((~np.isfinite(w)) | (w <= 1e-8), 1e3, r)
        k_grid = np.linspace(np.nanmin(k), np.nanmax(k), 25)
        w_grid = np.asarray(svi_w(k_grid, p[0], p[1], p[2], p[3], p[4]), dtype=float)
        pen = max(0.0, 1e-7 - float(np.nanmin(w_grid))) * 1e5
        return np.r_[r, pen]

    best = None
    for p0 in svi_starts(z, p_prev):
        t0 = tic()
        res = optimize.least_squares(
            err,
            np.clip(p0, lo + 1e-8, hi - 1e-8),
            bounds=(lo, hi),
            loss="soft_l1",
            f_scale=1.0,
            max_nfev=180,
            xtol=1e-8,
            ftol=1e-8,
        )
        item = {"res": res, "cost": float(res.cost), "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}
        if best is None or item["cost"] < best["cost"]:
            best = item
    return best["res"].x, best["res"].success, best["seconds"], best["res"].nfev, lo, hi
def fit_svi(q):
    p_rows = []
    f_rows = []
    d_rows = []
    p_prev = None
    for expiry, g in q.groupby("expiry", sort=True):
        g = g.sort_values("k").copy()
        tau = float(g["tau"].median())
        dte = float(g["dte_days"].median())
        if len(g) < min_quotes_per_expiry:
            d_rows.append({"expiry": expiry, "tau": tau, "dte_days": dte, "success": False, "n_quotes": len(g), "reason": "too few quotes"})
            continue
        p, ok, seconds, nfev, lo, hi = fit_svi_slice(g, p_prev)
        p_prev = p if ok else p_prev
        w_hat = np.asarray(svi_w(g["k"].to_numpy(dtype=float), *p), dtype=float)
        iv_hat = np.sqrt(np.maximum(w_hat, 1e-12) / g["tau"].to_numpy(dtype=float))
        px_hat = black76_price(g["option_type"].to_numpy(), g["forward"], g["strike"], g["tau"], iv_hat, g["discount_factor"])
        e_iv = iv_hat - g["iv_mid"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        e_w = w_hat - g["total_var"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        wt = g["weight"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        d_rows.append({
            "expiry": expiry,
            "tau": tau,
            "dte_days": dte,
            "success": bool(ok),
            "n_quotes": int(len(g)),
            "calibration_time": float(seconds),
            "objective_evaluations": int(nfev),
            "weighted_rmse_total_var": wrmse(e_w, wt),
            "weighted_rmse_iv": wrmse(e_iv, wt),
            "median_abs_iv_error": float(np.nanmedian(np.abs(e_iv))),
            "p90_abs_iv_error": float(np.nanquantile(np.abs(e_iv), 0.90)),
            "min_fitted_total_var": float(np.nanmin(w_hat)),
            "parameter_at_bound": near_bound(p, lo, hi),
            "wing_warning": bool(np.nanmin(w_hat) <= 1e-6),
            "reason": "ok" if ok else "optimizer failed",
        })
        p_rows.append({"expiry": expiry, "tau": tau, "dte_days": dte, "a": p[0], "b": p[1], "rho": p[2], "m": p[3], "sigma": p[4], "success": bool(ok)})
        z = g.copy()
        z["model"] = "svi"
        z["model_total_var"] = w_hat
        z["model_iv"] = iv_hat
        z["model_price"] = np.asarray(px_hat, dtype=float)
        z["iv_residual"] = z["model_iv"] - z["iv_mid"]
        z["price_residual"] = z["model_price"] - z["mid"]
        f_rows.append(z)
    fit = pd.concat(f_rows, ignore_index=True) if f_rows else pd.DataFrame()
    return pd.DataFrame(p_rows), fit, pd.DataFrame(d_rows)
t0 = tic()

The SVI diagnostic table is excellent. The first displayed expiries all succeed, and many weighted IV RMSE values are tiny. For example, several short expiries have weighted IV RMSE around 0.0005 to 0.0011, and even the weaker short slice shown has about 0.0039. Median absolute IV errors are mostly below one vol point and often only a few basis points of vol.

The fitted-smile plot confirms this visually: SVI follows the market smiles closely across the selected high-support expiries. The residual scatter is centered around zero and mostly tight. The few larger residuals appear in thinner parts of the wing, which is expected because tails are harder to fit and quotes are less dense there.

The parameter-term plots show that SVI is flexible but also noisy. Some parameters move irregularly across maturity. That is the classic SVI tradeoff: slice-level flexibility gives excellent fit, but it doesn’t automatically guarantee a smooth, arbitrage-aware surface across maturities.

Reading SVI Residuals Like a Surface Diagnostic

SVI residuals aren’t only a measure of fit. Their pattern tells us what kind of surface feature the model struggles with.

If residuals are randomly scattered around zero, the model is flexible enough and remaining errors are mostly quote noise. If residuals form a pattern by \(k\), the smile shape is wrong. If residuals form a pattern by maturity, the term structure is unstable. If residuals are concentrated in one wing, the model is underfitting tail curvature.

In the displayed residual scatter, most observations are close to zero, with a few larger wing misses. That pattern is healthy for a per-expiry surface model. It tells us SVI is strong enough to act as the fair-value core, while still leaving tails as the natural place to watch model disagreement.

The parameter-term plots are also useful. Smooth parameter paths across maturity would be ideal, but the output shows some movement and noise. We shouldn’t overinterpret individual SVI parameters at one expiry. The fitted surface and residuals are more reliable than a narrative about one noisy parameter series.

8) SSVI: Global Surface Discipline

SVI fits each expiry separately. SSVI adds a global structure across maturities. Instead of giving each expiry its own five parameters, SSVI expresses the total variance smile through the ATM total variance \(\theta\) and a smaller set of global parameters.

The form we use is:

\[ w(k,\theta)=\frac{\theta}{2}\left(1+\rho\phi(\theta)k+\sqrt{(\phi(\theta)k+\rho)^2+1-\rho^2}\right) \]

where:

  • \(\theta\) is the ATM total variance for that expiry,
  • \(\rho\) controls skew direction,
  • \(\phi(\theta)\) controls how skew intensity changes with maturity,
  • \(\eta\) and \(\gamma\) parameterize \(\phi\).

The implementation uses:

\[ \phi(\theta)=\frac{\eta}{\theta^\gamma(1+\theta)^{1-\gamma}} \]

The model has a clear economic interpretation:

  • \(\theta\) says how much variance the market prices at the center for each maturity.
  • \(\rho\) says whether downside or upside strikes are more expensive.
  • \(\eta\) controls how steep the smile is.
  • \(\gamma\) controls how that steepness decays or changes as total variance grows with maturity.

This is more restrictive than SVI. That restriction is useful when we want a smooth surface, but it can be costly when the actual market has maturity-specific irregularities.

The Role of \(\theta\) in SSVI

The key SSVI idea is to separate the surface into:

  1. ATM total variance by maturity,
  2. a global rule that shapes the smile around it.

The ATM total variance is:

\[ \theta(T)=\sigma_{ATM}^2(T)T \]

If \(\theta\) rises with maturity, the total variance budget rises. SSVI then asks how skew changes as that total variance budget changes. That is much more structured than fitting every expiry independently.

The function:

\[ \phi(\theta)=\frac{\eta}{\theta^\gamma(1+\theta)^{1-\gamma}} \]

makes skew level depend on maturity. When \(\theta\) is small, short maturity smiles can be steep. When \(\theta\) is large, longer maturity smiles usually become smoother. The parameter \(\gamma\) controls how quickly that transition happens.

This helps with calendar stability because the model ties smiles together through \(\theta(T)\). If the 21-day and 30-day smiles are very different, SSVI doesn’t freely fit both unless the ATM total variance curve and global parameters justify it. That can reduce overfitting, especially for sparse or noisy surfaces.

The cost is bias. Real SPX smiles can have expiration-specific effects, event risk, dealer positioning, and liquidity shocks. SSVI smooths through some of those details.

def theta_from_atm(q):
    rows = []
    for expiry, g in q.groupby("expiry", sort=True):
        near = g[np.abs(g["k"]) <= 0.045].copy()
        use = near if len(near) >= 3 else g.iloc[np.argsort(np.abs(g["k"].to_numpy(dtype=float)))[: min(5, len(g))]].copy()
        wt = np.maximum(use["weight"].to_numpy(dtype=float), 1e-8)
        theta = float(np.average(use["total_var"].to_numpy(dtype=float), weights=wt))
        rows.append({"expiry": expiry, "tau": float(g["tau"].median()), "dte_days": float(g["dte_days"].median()), "theta_ssvi": max(theta, 1e-8)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("tau").reset_index(drop=True)


@njit
def ssvi_w(k, theta, rho, eta, gamma):
    out = np.empty(k.size, dtype=np.float64)
    for i in range(k.size):
        th = max(theta[i], 1e-12)
        phi = eta / (th ** gamma * (1.0 + th) ** (1.0 - gamma))
        x = phi * k[i]
        inside = (x + rho) * (x + rho) + 1.0 - rho * rho
        out[i] = 0.5 * th * (1.0 + rho * x + math.sqrt(max(inside, 1e-12)))
    return out


t0 = tic()
_ = ssvi_w(np.array([0.0, 0.1]), np.array([0.02, 0.03]), -0.5, 1.0, 0.5)
ssvi_compile_time = toc("compile ssvi", t0, 2)
def fit_ssvi(q):
    theta_curve = theta_from_atm(q)
    z = q.merge(theta_curve[["expiry", "theta_ssvi"]], on="expiry", how="left").copy()
    k = z["k"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    theta = z["theta_ssvi"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    y = z["total_var"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    eps = z["eps_w"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    eps_med = float(np.nanmedian(eps[np.isfinite(eps) & (eps > 0)])) if np.isfinite(eps).any() else 1e-4
    eps = np.clip(eps, max(1e-5, 0.25 * eps_med), 0.25)
    root_wt = np.sqrt(z["weight"].to_numpy(dtype=float))
    lo = np.array([-0.999, 0.001, 0.00])
    hi = np.array([0.999, 25.000, 1.00])

    def err(p):
        w = np.asarray(ssvi_w(k, theta, p[0], p[1], p[2]), dtype=float)
        r = root_wt * (w - y) / eps
        r = np.where((~np.isfinite(w)) | (w <= 1e-8), 1e3, r)
        return np.r_[r, max(0.0, 1e-8 - float(np.nanmin(w))) * 1e5]

    starts = [np.array([-0.55, 1.2, 0.50]), np.array([-0.75, 2.0, 0.35]), np.array([-0.35, 0.8, 0.70]), np.array([0.05, 1.0, 0.50])]
    best = None
    for p0 in starts:
        t0 = tic()
        res = optimize.least_squares(
            err,
            np.clip(p0, lo + 1e-8, hi - 1e-8),
            bounds=(lo, hi),
            loss="soft_l1",
            f_scale=1.0,
            max_nfev=160,
            xtol=1e-8,
            ftol=1e-8,
        )
        item = {"res": res, "cost": float(res.cost), "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}
        if best is None or item["cost"] < best["cost"]:
            best = item
    return best["res"].x, theta_curve, best["res"].success, best["seconds"], best["res"].nfev, lo, hi
t0 = tic()
p_ssvi, theta_curve, ok_ssvi, seconds_ssvi, nfev_ssvi, lo_ssvi, hi_ssvi = fit_ssvi(q0)
toc("calibrate ssvi", t0, len(q0))
ssvi_params = pd.DataFrame([{"rho": p_ssvi[0], "eta": p_ssvi[1], "gamma": p_ssvi[2], "success": bool(ok_ssvi), "calibration_time": seconds_ssvi, "objective_evaluations": int(nfev_ssvi), "parameter_at_bound": near_bound(p_ssvi, lo_ssvi, hi_ssvi)}])
ssvi_fit = q0.merge(theta_curve[["expiry", "theta_ssvi"]], on="expiry", how="left").copy()
ssvi_fit["model"] = "ssvi"
ssvi_fit["model_total_var"] = ssvi_w(ssvi_fit["k"].to_numpy(dtype=float), ssvi_fit["theta_ssvi"].to_numpy(dtype=float), *p_ssvi)
ssvi_fit["model_iv"] = np.sqrt(np.maximum(ssvi_fit["model_total_var"], 1e-12) / ssvi_fit["tau"])
ssvi_fit["model_price"] = black76_price(ssvi_fit["option_type"].to_numpy(), ssvi_fit["forward"], ssvi_fit["strike"], ssvi_fit["tau"], ssvi_fit["model_iv"], ssvi_fit["discount_factor"])
ssvi_fit["iv_residual"] = ssvi_fit["model_iv"] - ssvi_fit["iv_mid"]
ssvi_fit["price_residual"] = ssvi_fit["model_price"] - ssvi_fit["mid"]
ssvi_by_expiry = ssvi_fit.groupby("expiry").apply(lambda g: pd.Series({"dte_days": float(g["dte_days"].median()), "n_quotes": int(len(g)), "weighted_rmse_iv": wrmse(g["iv_residual"], g["weight"]), "median_abs_iv_error": float(np.nanmedian(np.abs(g["iv_residual"])))})).reset_index()
ssvi_diag = pd.DataFrame([{
    "success": bool(ok_ssvi),
    "n_quotes": int(len(ssvi_fit)),
    "weighted_rmse_total_var": wrmse(ssvi_fit["model_total_var"] - ssvi_fit["total_var"], ssvi_fit["weight"]),
    "weighted_rmse_iv": wrmse(ssvi_fit["iv_residual"], ssvi_fit["weight"]),
    "median_abs_iv_error": float(np.nanmedian(np.abs(ssvi_fit["iv_residual"]))),
    "p90_abs_iv_error": float(np.nanquantile(np.abs(ssvi_fit["iv_residual"]), 0.90)),
    "smoothness_score": float(np.nanstd(np.diff(theta_curve["theta_ssvi"], n=2))) if len(theta_curve) >= 3 else np.nan,
    "calibration_time": float(seconds_ssvi),
    "objective_evaluations": int(nfev_ssvi),
    "parameter_at_bound": bool(ssvi_params.loc[0, "parameter_at_bound"]),
}])

The SSVI fit returns \(\rho\approx -0.497\), \(\eta\approx 2.98\), and \(\gamma\approx 0.31\), with success and no parameter-bound warning. The negative \(\rho\) is exactly what we expect for SPX: downside skew is structurally expensive.

Fit quality is weaker than raw SVI: weighted IV RMSE is around 0.0083, median absolute IV error around 0.0038, and P90 error around 0.0165. The residual heatmap shows this clearly. SSVI has systematic patches where it misses by maturity and moneyness bucket. That’s the price of global discipline.

This doesn’t make SSVI useless. It means SSVI is more of a surface regularizer than a pure best-fit machine. If we need a smooth arbitrage-aware surface representation, SSVI can be useful. If we need quote-level relative value signals, raw SVI is much sharper in this SPX snapshot.

When a Worse Fit Is Still Useful

SSVI’s larger error doesn’t make it useless. It gives us a different type of information. If SVI says an option is cheap but SSVI says that quote is only cheap because SVI is bending too much locally, then the trade is less convincing.

A rigid model can act as a regularization benchmark. We can think of SSVI as asking:

\[ \text{Can a globally disciplined surface explain this quote?} \]

SVI asks:

\[ \text{Can a flexible local smile explain this quote?} \]

If both agree that the quote is rich or cheap, the residual is more robust. If only the flexible model sees it, the residual may just be an artifact of local overfitting.

That is why the later ensemble gives SSVI a tiny weight rather than zero. It is too biased for primary pricing, but it can still contribute model disagreement and discipline.

The SVI-versus-SSVI error plot makes the tradeoff visible. SVI errors stay close to zero across maturities, while SSVI errors are much larger at the short end and remain above SVI through most of the term structure. The shape is economically informative: short-maturity SPX smiles often have event risk, crash protection demand, and discrete supply-demand imbalances that a global three-parameter structure can’t fully absorb.

A clean reading is:

  • SVI is better for local quote-level pricing on this day.
  • SSVI is better for enforcing a coherent global surface shape.
  • Using SSVI alone for trading residuals would create many false signals because some residuals are just model rigidity.

9) SABR: Stochastic Smile Dynamics Through an Approximation

SABR is the first model here that has true stochastic-volatility dynamics behind its smile formula. The standard SABR dynamics for a forward \(F_t\) are:

\[ dF_t=\alpha_t F_t^\beta dW_t^F \]

\[ d\alpha_t=\nu\alpha_t dW_t^\alpha \]

with correlation:

\[ dW_t^F dW_t^\alpha=\rho dt \]

The parameters mean:

  • \(F_t\) is the forward price.
  • \(\alpha_t\) is the instantaneous volatility scale.
  • \(\beta\) controls how volatility changes with the level of the forward.
  • \(\nu\) is volatility-of-volatility.
  • \(\rho\) controls the skew through correlation between forward shocks and volatility shocks.

If \(\rho<0\), a negative forward move tends to come with a positive volatility shock. That creates left skew, which is exactly the equity-index behavior we usually see.

SABR is usually used through an approximate implied-volatility formula. We don’t simulate the SABR process here. We fit the implied-volatility approximation to the market smile. The model is dynamic in motivation but fast in implementation.

Hagan-Style SABR Implied Volatility

The full SABR process doesn’t have a simple exact closed-form implied-volatility formula for every case, so practitioners often use the Hagan approximation. The formula is built around:

\[ z=\frac{\nu}{\alpha}(FK)^{(1-\beta)/2}\log\!\left(\frac{F}{K}\right) \]

and:

\[ x(z)=\log\left(\frac{\sqrt{1-2\rho z+z^2}+z-\rho}{1-\rho}\right) \]

The implied volatility is roughly an ATM scaling term multiplied by a correction involving \(z/x(z)\) and maturity adjustments. The exact expression is more involved, but the intuition is clean:

  • \(\alpha\) sets the ATM volatility level,
  • \(\beta\) controls how the level changes with the forward,
  • \(\rho\) controls skew through spot-vol correlation,
  • \(\nu\) controls curvature through volatility-of-volatility.

Near ATM, \(\log(F/K)\) is close to zero, so \(z\) is close to zero and the formula behaves smoothly. Away from ATM, \(z/x(z)\) adjusts the vol to create skew and curvature.

This is why SABR is popular: it gives a fast implied-volatility formula with parameters that still have dynamic meaning. It sits between a pure surface fit and a full Monte Carlo stochastic-volatility model.

SABR and Smile Movement

SABR became popular partly because it gives more realistic smile movement than simple local-volatility intuition. The core reason is that volatility has its own random driver and is correlated with the forward.

If the forward falls and \(\rho<0\), volatility tends to rise. That means the smile can move with the underlying in a way that looks closer to observed equity and rate markets. This is a dynamic statement about how the smile moves with the underlying.

In formula form, the covariance between the forward shock and volatility shock is:

\[ \text{Cov}(dF_t,d\alpha_t)=\alpha_t^2\nu F_t^\beta \rho\,dt \]

When \(\rho\) is negative, negative forward moves are associated with positive volatility moves. That creates skew and affects hedging. A delta hedge derived from a model with stochastic smile movement can behave differently from one derived from a sticky-strike or sticky-delta rule.

We don’t build the full dynamic SABR hedging system here. We use SABR as a structural smile model, but understanding its dynamic origin helps explain why it is more meaningful than a generic curve fit.

SABR Parameter Intuition

The parameter \(\beta\) deserves careful explanation. It controls the elasticity of volatility to the forward level.

  • If \(\beta=0\), the forward has approximately normal volatility. Absolute price moves are more stable.
  • If \(\beta=1\), the forward has lognormal volatility. Percentage moves are more stable.
  • If \(0<\beta<1\), the model sits between normal and lognormal behavior.

For equity index options, \(\beta=1\) can be natural because prices are often modeled in log-return space. But equity smiles can be better fit by lower beta values because the model then gets a different balance between skew and curvature.

The fitted SABR formula is sensitive to \(\rho\) and \(\nu\):

  • More negative \(\rho\) steepens downside skew.
  • Larger \(\nu\) increases smile curvature because volatility itself can move more violently.

For example, two SABR smiles can have the same ATM volatility but different wing behavior. A higher \(\nu\) makes both wings more expensive because future volatility is more uncertain. A more negative \(\rho\) makes the left wing more expensive than the right wing because bad spot moves tend to coincide with higher volatility.

SABR Calibration by Expiry

SABR is usually fitted slice by slice, just like SVI. For a fixed expiry, the target is implied volatility:

\[ \min_{\alpha,\rho,\nu}\sum_i \omega_i\left(\frac{\sigma_{SABR}(F,K_i,T;\alpha,\beta,\rho,\nu)-\sigma_i^{mkt}}{\epsilon_{\sigma,i}}\right)^2 \]

In this project, \(\beta\) is chosen from a small grid and then held fixed inside each slice fit. This is common because \(\beta\) can be weakly identified. If we try to estimate \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\rho\), and \(\nu\) all at once for every expiry, the optimizer can trade off parameters in unstable ways.

The beta grid is:

\[ \beta\in \{0.5,\ 0.7,\ 1.0\} \]

Then we compare median errors and bound warnings. This is a disciplined approach: we don’t declare a favorite beta by theory alone; we let the surface say which beta gives the best stable fit.

SABR Versus SVI in Signal Design

SABR and SVI can both fit smiles, but they give different types of residual information.

SVI residuals are relative to a very flexible local curve. If a quote is far away from SVI, it is genuinely off the local smooth smile. SABR residuals are relative to a more structural stochastic-volatility approximation. If SABR misses a quote, the miss may reflect a real market irregularity or simply SABR’s lower flexibility.

Combining them is useful. If both models agree a quote is cheap, then the signal is more robust. If SVI says cheap but SABR says rich or fair, model disagreement rises and the total-error filter weakens the trade. This is exactly the kind of model-risk-aware behavior we want.

This is also why the ensemble weight is capped. SVI is strong enough to lead, but allowing a second model to contribute prevents the signal from being purely one-model residual chasing.

def sabr_iv_demo(f, k_strike, tau, alpha, beta, rho, nu):
    k_strike = np.asarray(k_strike, dtype=float)
    log_fk = np.log(np.clip(f / k_strike, 1e-12, None))
    fk_beta = (f * k_strike) ** ((1.0 - beta) / 2.0)
    z = (nu / max(alpha, 1e-12)) * fk_beta * log_fk
    xz = np.log((np.sqrt(1.0 - 2.0 * rho * z + z * z) + z - rho) / (1.0 - rho))
    z_xz = np.where(np.abs(z) < 1e-8, 1.0, z / xz)
    log_adj = 1.0 + ((1.0 - beta) ** 2 / 24.0) * log_fk ** 2 + ((1.0 - beta) ** 4 / 1920.0) * log_fk ** 4
    term = ((1.0 - beta) ** 2 / 24.0) * alpha ** 2 / np.maximum(fk_beta ** 2, 1e-12)
    term += 0.25 * rho * beta * nu * alpha / np.maximum(fk_beta, 1e-12)
    term += (2.0 - 3.0 * rho * rho) * nu * nu / 24.0
    return np.maximum(alpha / np.maximum(fk_beta * log_adj, 1e-12) * z_xz * (1.0 + term * tau), 1e-5)

The SABR demo plot shows these mechanisms. The first panel changes \(\alpha\) and lifts the smile. The second changes \(\rho\) and rotates the skew. The third changes \(\nu\) and changes smile convexity. This is a much more structural explanation than simply fitting a spline: parameters correspond to a hypothesized volatility process.

The beta grid chooses \(\beta=0.5\) as the primary setting. All three beta values succeed, but \(\beta=0.5\) gives the lowest median weighted IV RMSE, around 0.00203, compared with 0.00216 for \(\beta=0.7\) and 0.00236 for \(\beta=1.0\). There are no bound-share warnings for \(\rho\) or \(\nu\) in the displayed results.

That tells us SABR fits this SPX snapshot reasonably well, though still worse than raw SVI. That is expected: SVI is a flexible per-expiry smile machine, while SABR has a smaller and more structural parameter set.

@njit
def sabr_iv_hagan(fwd, strike, tau, alpha, beta, rho, nu):
    n = strike.size
    out = np.empty(n, dtype=np.float64)
    for i in range(n):
        f = max(fwd[i], 1e-12)
        k = max(strike[i], 1e-12)
        t = max(tau[i], 1e-12)
        a = max(alpha, 1e-12)
        b = beta
        r = min(max(rho, -0.999999), 0.999999)
        v = max(nu, 1e-12)
        log_fk = math.log(f / k)
        if abs(log_fk) < 1e-7:
            f_beta = f ** (1.0 - b)
            term = ((1.0 - b) ** 2 / 24.0) * a * a / max(f_beta * f_beta, 1e-12)
            term += 0.25 * r * b * v * a / max(f_beta, 1e-12)
            term += (2.0 - 3.0 * r * r) * v * v / 24.0
            out[i] = max(a / max(f_beta, 1e-12) * (1.0 + term * t), 1e-8)
        else:
            fk_beta = (f * k) ** ((1.0 - b) / 2.0)
            z = (v / a) * fk_beta * log_fk
            root = math.sqrt(max(1.0 - 2.0 * r * z + z * z, 1e-12))
            xz = math.log(max((root + z - r) / (1.0 - r), 1e-12))
            z_xz = 1.0 if abs(z) < 1e-8 or abs(xz) < 1e-10 else z / xz
            log_adj = 1.0 + ((1.0 - b) ** 2 / 24.0) * log_fk * log_fk + ((1.0 - b) ** 4 / 1920.0) * log_fk ** 4
            term = ((1.0 - b) ** 2 / 24.0) * a * a / max(fk_beta * fk_beta, 1e-12)
            term += 0.25 * r * b * v * a / max(fk_beta, 1e-12)
            term += (2.0 - 3.0 * r * r) * v * v / 24.0
            out[i] = max((a / max(fk_beta * log_adj, 1e-12)) * z_xz * (1.0 + term * t), 1e-8)
    return out
