The fair-value plot shows this filtering visually. Raw residuals exist across the surface, but once we account for entry spread and model disagreement, most points sit inside the no-trade zone. This is exactly what model-risk-aware relative value should do. A surface model will always produce residuals because real quotes are noisy. The useful question is whether those residuals exceed the uncertainty required to trade them.

Why the Watchlist Is Small

The small watchlist is a sign that the filters are strict. We start from a fitted surface with thousands of quotes, but after holdout scoring, spread adjustment, model disagreement, and error buffers, only a few quotes survive as watchlist candidates.

This is realistic for liquid SPX options. In a competitive market, obvious model-free mispricings shouldn’t appear everywhere. Most deviations from a fitted model are simply the market’s bid-ask, uncertainty, or a different model assumption.

The small watchlist also protects the later backtest. If the strategy selected hundreds of trades per day, the result would be dominated by correlated exposures and transaction costs. A sparse schedule gives a cleaner test of whether residuals have any useful information.

16) Historical Residual Validation

A model-selected residual only matters if it predicts something out of sample. We therefore fit trade models across historical signal dates and test whether residuals are related to next-day hedged P&L.

The validation object uses a next-day hedged payoff. The idea is:

  1. score a quote at date \(t\),
  2. hold it for one day,
  3. hedge delta exposure,
  4. subtract scheduled costs,
  5. check whether the residual direction predicted the next outcome.

A simple version of the payoff logic is:

\[ \Pi_{t+1}\approx q\,(V_{t+1}-V_t)-q\,\Delta_t(S_{t+1}-S_t)-\text{costs} \]

where:

  • \(q\) is position direction and quantity,
  • \(V\) is option value,
  • \(\Delta\) is option delta,
  • \(S\) is underlying spot or hedge instrument.

The delta hedge removes first-order spot exposure, so the remaining P&L is more about volatility, curvature, residual repricing, and model error. It is never perfectly pure because delta changes, volatility moves, spreads matter, and discrete hedging creates tracking error.

Spearman IC and Why Rank Matters

The validation uses rank correlation because residual magnitudes can be noisy. Spearman correlation asks whether larger signals tend to rank with better future outcomes. If \(R(z_i)\) is the rank of the residual score and \(R(\Pi_i)\) is the rank of future hedged payoff, then Spearman correlation is the Pearson correlation of those ranks:

\[ \rho_s=\text{Corr}(R(z_i),R(\Pi_i)) \]

This is more robust than raw correlation when the payoff distribution has outliers. Options have nonlinear payoffs, spreads, and jump moves, so rank-based diagnostics are often more stable.

The daily IC is the same idea applied date by date:

\[ IC_t=\rho_s(z_{i,t},\Pi_{i,t+1}) \]

Then training IC is a rolling estimate of whether the residual direction has recently worked. If training IC is negative, the residual sign is flipped. This is why the strategy can adapt when the model residual behaves more like a contrarian signal than a direct fair-value signal.

Training IC and Direction Learning

The signal direction is learned because residuals can behave in either direction. In theory, if a model says an option is cheap, buying it should make money as price converges upward. In practice, a residual can also indicate a risk premium or model bias. Then the profitable direction may be the opposite.

The rolling training IC estimates this:

\[ \widehat{IC}_{train,t}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{s=t-M}^{t-1}IC_s \]

The direction can be set as:

\[ d_t=\text{sign}(\widehat{IC}_{train,t}) \]

Then the effective score is:

\[ \tilde{z}_{i,t}=d_t z_{i,t} \]

If recent IC is negative, the strategy treats raw residuals as contrarian in the opposite direction. This is a very practical idea. It lets the data decide whether model residuals are converging or whether they are systematically pointing the wrong way under the current market microstructure.

Validation Sample Size and Dependence

The validation panel has many rows, but option rows are not independent in the same way stock returns might be. Quotes from the same date and same expiry share the same underlying move, volatility move, and liquidity environment. So 28,415 validation rows don’t mean 28,415 independent experiments.

This is why the daily IC series is important. It aggregates cross-sectional predictive behavior by date. The model can have many quote-level rows but still only about 504 daily environments. If the IC flips sign over time, the strategy has to adapt.

The decile table also has dependence. Options in the same decile can cluster by maturity or option type. So the validation results are evidence, but not final proof. The scheduled trade experiment is a stricter test because it samples a limited number of actual entries with spacing.

def fit_trade_models(q):
    p_svi, _, _ = fit_svi(q)
    p_sabr, _, _ = fit_sabr(q, primary_beta)
    p_ssvi = pd.DataFrame()
    theta_ssvi = pd.DataFrame()
    if ssvi_ok_for_trade:
        p, theta_ssvi, _, _, _, _, _ = fit_ssvi(q)
        p_ssvi = pd.DataFrame([{"rho": p[0], "eta": p[1], "gamma": p[2]}])
    return p_svi, p_ssvi, theta_ssvi, p_sabr


def score_date(q):
    q_anchor, q_holdout = holdout_split(q)
    if q_anchor.empty or q_holdout.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    p_svi, p_ssvi, theta_ssvi, p_sabr = fit_trade_models(q_anchor)
    out = q_holdout.copy()
    out["svi_iv"] = svi_iv_at(out, p_svi)
    out["svi_price"] = black76_price(out["option_type"].to_numpy(), out["forward"], out["strike"], out["tau"], out["svi_iv"], out["discount_factor"])
    cols = ["svi_price"]
    if sabr_in_signal:
        out["sabr_iv"] = sabr_iv_at(out, p_sabr, primary_beta)
        out["sabr_price"] = black76_price(out["option_type"].to_numpy(), out["forward"], out["strike"], out["tau"], out["sabr_iv"], out["discount_factor"])
        cols.append("sabr_price")
    if ssvi_ok_for_trade and not p_ssvi.empty:
        out["ssvi_iv"] = ssvi_iv_at(out, p_ssvi, theta_ssvi)
        out["ssvi_price"] = black76_price(out["option_type"].to_numpy(), out["forward"], out["strike"], out["tau"], out["ssvi_iv"], out["discount_factor"])
        cols.append("ssvi_price")
    weights = np.array([model_wt.get(c.replace("_price", ""), 0.0) for c in cols], dtype=float)
    weights = weights / max(float(weights.sum()), 1e-12)
    out["ensemble_price"] = np.zeros(len(out), dtype=float)
    for c, w in zip(cols, weights):
        out["ensemble_price"] += w * out[c]
    out["model_spread"] = out[cols].std(axis=1).fillna(0.0)
    out["price_residual"] = out["ensemble_price"] - out["mid"]
    out["spread_residual"] = out["price_residual"] / out["half_spread"].replace(0, np.nan)
    out["hedge_buffer"] = 0.0001 * np.abs(out["delta"].fillna(0.0)) * out["forward"] + 0.10 * out["half_spread"]
    out["total_error"] = (out["half_spread"] + 0.5 * out["expected_exit_half_spread"] + 0.5 * out["model_spread"] + out["hedge_buffer"]).clip(lower=0.02)
    out["z_residual"] = out["price_residual"] / out["total_error"].replace(0, np.nan)
    out["strict_candidate"] = out["z_residual"].abs() > 1.0
    out["watchlist_candidate"] = out["z_residual"].abs() > 0.5
    out["candidate"] = out["strict_candidate"]
    out["anchor_quotes"] = len(q_anchor)
    return out

def score_one_signal_date(d):
    d = pd.Timestamp(d).normalize()
    next_dates = all_dates[all_dates > np.datetime64(d)]
    if len(next_dates) == 0:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    d_next = pd.Timestamp(next_dates[0]).normalize()
    qd = calibration_panel[calibration_panel["date"].eq(d)].copy()
    scored = score_date(qd)
    if scored.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    q_next = quote_panel[quote_panel["date"].eq(d_next)].copy()
    q_next["next_mid"] = q_next["mid"]
    q_next["next_spot"] = q_next["spot"]
    q_next["next_half_spread"] = 0.5 * (q_next["ask"] - q_next["bid"]).clip(lower=0.0)
    m = scored.merge(q_next[["contract_id", "next_mid", "next_spot", "next_half_spread"]], on="contract_id", how="inner")
    m["next_date"] = d_next
    return m

    date_ic = validation_panel.groupby("date").apply(lambda g: g[["z_residual", "raw_hedged_pnl"]].corr(method="spearman").iloc[0, 1] if len(g) >= 5 else np.nan).rename("ic").reset_index()
    date_ic = date_ic.sort_values("date").reset_index(drop=True)

The validation run scores 504 signal dates and creates 28,415 validation rows. The Spearman correlations are negative for all residual scores:

  • raw residual: about -0.155,
  • spread-adjusted: about -0.144,
  • uncertainty-adjusted: about -0.147.

The negative sign means the raw residual direction needs to be interpreted carefully. The training IC column later flips signal direction based on recent performance. The daily IC table shows large variation: some dates have strongly positive IC, others strongly negative. By late 2023 the training IC is around -0.15, so the system learns that the residual should be traded in the opposite direction.

The decile table is more important than one correlation number. Mean next hedged P&L is positive in every decile, but the middle-positive residual deciles have the highest values, with hit rates above 70% in several bins. The highest \(z\) decile has lower mean P&L than mid-high deciles, which warns us that extreme residuals may include more model error or liquidity noise rather than cleaner opportunity.

Interpreting the Non-Monotonic Deciles

The decile table doesn’t show a perfect monotonic edge. That is important. In clean factor research, we often want higher signal deciles to produce higher future returns. Option residual trading is messier.

A mid-level residual can be tradable because it is large enough to matter but still inside a liquid, stable region. An extreme residual can be dangerous because it may come from:

  • stale quote,
  • low vega,
  • jump risk,
  • wide spread,
  • model extrapolation,
  • or a true market premium that doesn’t mean-revert.

So the fact that the middle-high deciles show strong hit rates while the highest decile weakens is economically believable. It tells us to use residuals with cost and model-risk gates rather than just buying the largest absolute residual.

The validation plots show three useful diagnostics:

  1. the distribution of daily ICs is wide,
  2. training IC evolves through time,
  3. decile performance isn’t monotonic in a clean textbook way.

That is a realistic result. Option relative value is noisy. A residual can mean mispricing, but it can also mean quote staleness, model misspecification, or temporary supply-demand pressure that doesn’t revert quickly. The validation layer stops the project from assuming every model residual is alpha.

17) Scheduled Delta-Hedged Trading Experiment

After validation, we run a scheduled trading experiment. The goal is to compare two entry selectors:

  • surface residual selector, which chooses trades based on the model residual logic,
  • matched ATM baseline, which chooses similar option type, date, sign, and maturity but targets a more ATM-like contract.

The residual strategy schedules up to 80 entries, spaced at least five trading days apart. This prevents the backtest from taking dozens of overlapping signals from the same date and pretending they are independent.

Each trade is held for three days. The backtest evaluates delta-hedged P&L with bid-ask and hedge costs. The delta hedge is meant to reduce directional exposure:

\[ \text{hedge shares}\approx -q\Delta \]

If we are long one call with \(\Delta=0.45\), we short about \(0.45\) units of the underlying per option multiplier. If the index rises, the call gains but the short hedge loses. The remaining P&L comes from volatility movement, gamma, theta, residual convergence, and execution costs.

Delta-Hedged P&L Through a Taylor Expansion

The delta-hedged P&L can be understood through the option’s local expansion:

\[ dV \approx \Delta dS+\frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2+\mathcal{V}d\sigma+\Theta dt+\text{higher-order terms} \]

If we hedge with \(-\Delta\) units of the underlying, the first-order spot term is reduced:

\[ dV-\Delta dS \approx \frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2+\mathcal{V}d\sigma+\Theta dt+\text{hedging error} \]

This is why the hedged strategy is still risky. It removes first-order direction, but it leaves:

  • gamma exposure to realized movement,
  • vega exposure to implied-volatility changes,
  • theta decay,
  • residual convergence or divergence,
  • re-hedging costs,
  • bid-ask costs,
  • discrete hedging error.

A relative-value option signal is usually trying to earn from residual convergence after controlling delta. It is not guaranteed to be positive because gamma/theta/vega can dominate over a short holding period.

Gamma, Theta, and Vega Interactions

A three-day option trade can lose money even when the fair-value residual is correct because the Greeks interact.

If we buy a cheap option, we are usually long gamma and long vega:

\[ \Gamma>0,\quad \mathcal{V}>0 \]

Long gamma benefits from realized movement:

\[ \frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2 \]

Long vega benefits from implied volatility rising:

\[ \mathcal{V}d\sigma \]

But long options usually pay theta:

\[ \Theta dt<0 \]

and the bid-ask spread is paid at entry and exit. So the residual has to converge fast enough to beat theta and costs. Short options reverse these exposures: they collect theta but suffer from gamma and vega shocks.

This is why residual trading is difficult. A model can identify a cheap option, but the position still has Greek exposures over the holding window. The hedged backtest is needed because static residual ranking alone can’t answer that.

P&L Components

The attribution is split into:

\[ \Pi_{\text{net}}=\Pi_{\text{option mid}}+\Pi_{\text{delta hedge}}-\text{bid-ask and hedge costs} \]

where:

  • \(\Pi_{\text{option mid}}\) is the change in option mid prices,
  • \(\Pi_{\text{delta hedge}}\) is the P&L from rebalancing the underlying hedge,
  • costs include option entry/exit spread and hedge trading costs.

This decomposition is important because a strategy can look bad for different reasons:

  • the option signal can be wrong,
  • the delta hedge can lose money,
  • costs can overwhelm a small edge,
  • the selected options can carry too much vega or gamma risk.

A model-based strategy that produces lower gross loss and lower exposure than the matched baseline can still lose net money if spreads and hedging costs are too large.

Why a Matched Baseline Is Needed

A model-selected option can have a different delta, maturity, spread, and vega than a generic option. If we compare it only against zero, we can’t tell whether the result came from the residual signal or from general option exposure.

The matched baseline solves this by choosing an option with similar broad characteristics but without the residual-selection logic. The comparison asks:

\[ \text{incremental value}=\Pi_{\text{residual selector}}-\Pi_{\text{matched baseline}} \]

A good residual selector should either:

  • earn more than the matched baseline,
  • lose less than the matched baseline,
  • reduce drawdown for similar exposure,
  • or show better attribution after hedging.

In the SPX run, it mainly loses less. That is still useful evidence because it means the residual filter is removing some bad exposures, even though it hasn’t created a positive net edge under this simple three-day schedule.

def take_chronological_entries(x, min_gap_days=5, max_entries=80):
    rows = []
    last_date = None
    x = x.sort_values("date").copy()
    for _, r in x.iterrows():
        d = pd.Timestamp(r["date"]).normalize()
        if last_date is None or (d - last_date).days >= int(min_gap_days):
            rows.append(r)
            last_date = d
        if len(rows) >= int(max_entries):
            break
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).reset_index(drop=True) if rows else pd.DataFrame()

entry_day_quotes["dte"] = entry_day_quotes["dte_days"]

entry_day_quotes["half_spread"] = 0.5 * (entry_day_quotes["ask"] - entry_day_quotes["bid"]).clip(lower=0.0)
entry_day_quotes["timestamp"] = entry_day_quotes["date"]

if not entry_day_quotes.empty:
    candidate_keys = entry_day_quotes["contract_key"].unique()
    first_future = pd.Timestamp(entry_dates.min()).normalize() if len(entry_dates) else pd.NaT
    last_future = pd.Timestamp(entry_dates.max()).normalize() + pd.Timedelta(days=18) if len(entry_dates) else pd.NaT
    future_counts = quote_panel[
        quote_panel["contract_key"].isin(candidate_keys)
        & quote_panel["date"].between(first_future, last_future)
    ][["date", "contract_key"]].drop_duplicates(["date", "contract_key"]).copy()
    future_counts = future_counts.sort_values(["contract_key", "date"])
    future_counts["future_quote_count"] = future_counts.groupby("contract_key").cumcount(ascending=False) + 1
    entry_day_quotes = entry_day_quotes.merge(future_counts, on=["date", "contract_key"], how="left")
else:
    entry_day_quotes["future_quote_count"] = pd.Series(dtype=float)

    for d, g in entry_day_quotes.groupby("date", sort=False)
}

def pick_matched_baseline(day, option_type, target_dte):
    want = day[day["option_type"].eq(option_type)].copy()
    if want.empty:
        return None
    target_dte = float(target_dte) if np.isfinite(target_dte) else 35.0
    lo = max(7.0, target_dte - 10.0)
    hi = min(90.0, target_dte + 10.0)
    d = want[want["dte_days"].between(lo, hi) & want["delta"].abs().between(0.25, 0.75)].copy()
    if d.empty:
        d = want[want["dte_days"].between(max(7.0, target_dte - 18.0), min(90.0, target_dte + 18.0)) & want["delta"].abs().between(0.20, 0.80)].copy()
    if d.empty:
        d = want[want["dte_days"].between(21.0, 60.0) & want["delta"].abs().between(0.20, 0.80)].copy()
    if d.empty:
        return None
    volume = pd.to_numeric(d["volume"], errors="coerce").fillna(0.0) if "volume" in d.columns else pd.Series(0.0, index=d.index)
    future = pd.to_numeric(d["future_quote_count"], errors="coerce").fillna(0.0) if "future_quote_count" in d.columns else pd.Series(0.0, index=d.index)
    d["entry_score"] = (
        -2.0 * (d["delta"].abs() - 0.50).abs()
        -0.06 * (d["dte_days"] - target_dte).abs()
        -1.75 * d["relative_spread"].fillna(0.0)
        +0.00015 * volume
        +0.015 * future
    )
    return d.sort_values("entry_score", ascending=False).iloc[0]

def normalized_rows(run_name, result):
    s = summarize_hedging_backtest(result).copy()
    c = result.get("components", pd.DataFrame()).copy()
    if s.empty or c.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    c = c.sort_values(["strategy", "episode_id", "date"])
    first = c.groupby(["strategy", "episode_id"], as_index=False).head(1).copy()
    first["entry_premium"] = (first["main_pos"].abs() * first["option_mid"].abs() * option_multiplier).replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    first["initial_abs_vega"] = first["vega_after"].abs().replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    first["initial_abs_delta"] = first["delta_after"].abs().replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    den = first.groupby("strategy").agg(
        entry_premium=("entry_premium", "sum"),
        initial_abs_vega=("initial_abs_vega", "sum"),
        initial_abs_delta=("initial_abs_delta", "sum"),
        episodes=("episode_id", "nunique"),
    ).reset_index()
    avg_delta = c.groupby("strategy")["delta_after"].apply(lambda x: float(np.nanmean(np.abs(x)))).rename("average_abs_delta").reset_index()
    out = s.merge(den, on="strategy", how="left").merge(avg_delta, on="strategy", how="left")
    out["run"] = run_name
    out["pnl_per_option_premium"] = out["total_pnl"] / out["entry_premium"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    out["pnl_per_traded_notional"] = out["total_pnl"] / out["traded_notional"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    out["pnl_per_initial_vega"] = out["total_pnl"] / out["initial_abs_vega"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    out["pnl_per_average_abs_delta"] = out["total_pnl"] / out["average_abs_delta"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    out["cost_pct_premium"] = out["total_costs"] / out["entry_premium"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    out["max_drawdown_per_notional"] = out["max_drawdown"] / out["traded_notional"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    return out

The schedule table shows 80 residual entries and 80 matched baseline entries, with a same-type match rate of 100%. That gives a fair comparison: the matched strategy isn’t a random portfolio; it is designed to share broad trade characteristics with the residual schedule.

The hedge-book summary shows 160 scheduled entries and 6,658 hedge-book rows across 159 contracts. The residual strategy and matched strategy both have enough marks to run.

The performance table is sobering:

  • matched ATM delta strategy loses about $26,621,
  • surface residual delta strategy loses about $9,032,
  • both are negative after costs,
  • the residual strategy has lower drawdown and much lower traded notional.

So the model-selected residual strategy improves materially over the matched ATM baseline, but it still doesn’t produce a positive net strategy in this configuration. That is a much stronger conclusion than simply saying “the model worked.” The signal has some selection value, but trading frictions and short-horizon option noise are still too strong.

Exposure Differences Between Residual and Matched Trades

The matched baseline trades much larger notional than the residual strategy: about $37.37 million traded notional for matched ATM versus about $4.80 million for surface residual. That difference is material. It means the residual selector naturally chooses a different exposure profile.

Mean absolute delta after hedging is also much lower for the residual strategy, around 8.0 versus 28.7. Mean absolute vega is lower too, around 17,677 versus 45,980.

So the residual selector isn’t only changing entry direction. It is changing the risk footprint of selected options. The strategy loses less partly because it takes smaller and more controlled exposures. That is a valid risk-management benefit, even though the net P&L remains negative.

Reading Negative P&L Honestly

The scheduled backtest losing money is not something to hide. It is one of the strongest parts of the project because it prevents overclaiming.

A model can be useful and still fail as a naive trading strategy. The SPX residual selector:

  • loses much less than the matched baseline,
  • has lower notional,
  • has lower absolute delta after hedging,
  • has lower vega,
  • has lower total cost,
  • still loses net money.

That combination says the model is doing some useful selection, but the execution rule is not yet strong enough. Possible reasons include:

  • three-day horizon is too short or too long,
  • thresholds are too loose,
  • spreads are too expensive,
  • signals are too small,
  • delta hedging is too crude,
  • residual direction is unstable.

This kind of diagnosis is much better than tuning parameters until the P&L turns positive. The output gives a realistic research conclusion.

The normalized performance table shows the residual strategy has worse P&L per option premium than the matched baseline, but it uses much less notional and has smaller absolute losses. The cost percentage of premium is higher for the residual strategy, around 3.4% versus 1.8% for the matched baseline, which means it trades options where spreads are more painful relative to premium.

The attribution table is very useful:

  • matched ATM option mid P&L is about -$17,135,
  • residual option mid P&L is about -$13,475,
  • residual delta hedge P&L is much better, around +$8,446 versus +$3,594,
  • residual costs are much lower, around $3,910 versus $14,372.

This explains why the residual strategy loses less. It isn’t because every option residual converges. It is because the selected trades have better hedge behavior and lower total cost exposure than the matched baseline.

The fixed-hold equity curve plot confirms the table. Both strategies draw down, but the matched ATM baseline loses more and has a much larger drawdown. The residual selector is less damaging and more controlled. That still matters for research: a relative-value model can first prove that it selects better bad trades before it becomes good enough to generate positive trades.

For a production-style version, the next improvements would be tighter entry thresholds, fewer trades, more liquidity constraints, and perhaps longer or adaptive holding windows. We don’t add those here because the point of this project is model comparison and signal validation, not overfitting a trading rule until it looks good.

18) Object Inventory Before the Library Repeat

The object inventory confirms the project scale:

  • about 1.5 million calibration-panel rows,
  • about 1.52 million model-panel rows,
  • SVI diagnostics across 29 expiries,
  • SABR diagnostics across 87 beta/expiry combinations,
  • compact Merton, Heston, and Bates diagnostics,
  • more than 28,000 validation rows,
  • scheduled entry tables,
  • hedge-book components,
  • normalized performance outputs.

This matters because Project 11 isn’t just a model demo. It is an end-to-end modeling stack:

\[ \text{quotes}\rightarrow \text{models}\rightarrow \text{fair values}\rightarrow \text{validation}\rightarrow \text{hedged P\&L} \]

Each arrow can fail. The project includes diagnostics at every arrow so we can see where the edge weakens.

19) Secondary Application: BTC Options with the Library

The final section repeats the workflow through the library on BTC options. The data folders are:

  • BTC/Deribit option-chain source and builder: data/btc_optionsdx
  • BTC spot source and downloader: data/btc_yfinance
  • Treasury yields for discounting: data/us_treasury_yields

BTC is a much harder market than SPX for this kind of workflow. The surface has wider wings, fewer institutional-style quote regularities, 24/7 trading, different settlement conventions, and a much more jump-sensitive underlying. The same model stack therefore faces a different economic problem:

  • SPX smiles are dominated by downside equity crash protection and structured product flows.
  • BTC smiles often reflect jump risk in both directions, leverage liquidations, weekend gap risk, and unstable liquidity.
  • Delta hedging is harder because the underlying trades continuously but option marks can be missing or irregular.

This makes BTC a strong stress test for the library version.

Why BTC Changes the Model Hierarchy

BTC options force the same models into a different volatility ecosystem.

SPX has a structurally persistent downside skew because investors buy crash protection and dealers manage equity-index risk. BTC can have much more two-sided jump risk: upside squeezes, downside liquidations, weekend gaps, exchange-specific liquidity effects, and sharp volatility repricings.

That changes which model families look useful:

  • Merton-style jumps can become more competitive because discontinuous moves are central to BTC.
  • Heston can struggle if the surface wants abrupt jumps rather than continuous variance shocks.
  • SSVI can struggle because one global smooth surface discipline may be too restrictive.
  • SVI can still fit well, but its static fit doesn’t guarantee tradability.
  • SABR can help as a structural fast check, especially when \(\beta=1\) is used for lognormal-style crypto moves.

The secondary implementation is therefore a real market stress test: it checks whether the same architecture adapts when the market’s volatility economics change.

BTC Surface Economics

BTC options tend to price several risks that are less central in SPX:

  • weekend movement while traditional markets are closed,
  • liquidation cascades from leverage,
  • exchange-specific liquidity changes,
  • jumps after ETF, regulatory, or macro headlines,
  • volatility demand from both upside and downside speculation,
  • unstable term structure when spot trends strongly.

This can make BTC smiles less smooth and less one-sided than SPX. In SPX, the left wing is often structurally rich. In BTC, both tails can matter depending on the regime. A huge upside squeeze can be just as important as a crash in some periods.

That is why Merton performs strongly in the BTC common benchmark. A jump distribution is a natural language for a market where discontinuities and gap risk are central.

The library implementation runs the same main components:

  1. clean BTC option quotes,
  2. attach BTC spot and U.S. rates,
  3. infer forwards from parity,
  4. compute IVs and Greeks,
  5. fit SVI, SSVI, SABR, Merton, Heston, and Bates,
  6. compare model errors and runtime,
  7. validate residual scores,
  8. schedule residual and matched baseline trades,
  9. run unhedged and delta-hedged backtests under 24/7 crypto calendar assumptions.

The forward fallback share is only about 0.053%, meaning parity inference works for almost all rows. That is important because BTC option data can be messy, and a high fallback share would make model coordinates less reliable.

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda x: f"{x:,.6f}")
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 120)

colors = ["#069AF3", "#FE420F", "#00008B", "#008080", "#CC79A7", "#DC143C", "#9614fa", "#0072B2", "#7BC8F6", "#04D8B2", "#800080", "#FF8072"]
plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"] = cycler(color=colors)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 3.5), "figure.dpi": 300, "savefig.dpi": 250, "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.20, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.titlesize": 11, "axes.labelsize": 10, "xtick.labelsize": 9, "ytick.labelsize": 9, "legend.fontsize": 8})

engine = "auto"
ann_days = 365.25
random_state = 7

root = Path.cwd()
if root.name.lower() == "notebooks":
    root = root.parent

data_dir = root / "data"

backend_report = choose_model_engine(engine=engine)
display(backend_report)

btc_spot = load_ohlcv(
    data_dir / "btc_usd_ohlcv.csv",
    source="yfinance_csv",
    fields=("close",),
)
btc_spot = btc_spot["close"].rename("BTC")
btc_spot = btc_spot[btc_spot > 0]

btc_options = load_option_chain(
    data_dir / "btc_options_chain.parquet",
    source="btc_deribit",
    annualization_days=365.0,
)

us_rates = load_par_yield_curve(
    data_dir / "us_treasury_yields.csv",
    source="us_treasury",
)

btc_quotes = attach_spot_from_series(
    btc_options,
    btc_spot,
    date_col="date",
    spot_col="spot",
    method="previous",
    overwrite=False,
)
btc_quotes = convert_quotes_to_usd_equivalent(
    btc_quotes,
    spot_col="spot",
    price_cols=("bid", "ask", "mid", "last", "mark"),
    unit="auto",
    contract_size=1.0,
)

clean_quotes, clean_report = clean_option_quotes(
    btc_quotes,
    min_dte=3,
    max_dte=180,
    moneyness_range=(0.45, 1.75),
    max_relative_spread=0.60,
    closest_atm_pairs=None,
    min_pairs_per_expiry=0,
    annualization_days=365.0,
)

rate_start = clean_quotes["date"].min() - pd.Timedelta(days=30)
rate_end = clean_quotes["date"].max()
us_rates = us_rates.loc[(us_rates.index >= rate_start) & (us_rates.index <= rate_end)].copy()

clean_quotes = attach_rates(
    clean_quotes,
    us_rates,
    date_col="date",
    tau_col="tau",
    out_col="rate",
)
clean_quotes = add_discount_factors(
    clean_quotes,
    rate_col="rate",
    tau_col="tau",
    out_col="discount_factor",
)
clean_quotes = infer_forwards_from_parity(
    clean_quotes,
    date_col="date",
    expiry_col="expiry",
    strike_col="strike",
    option_type_col="option_type",
    mid_col="mid",
    discount_col="discount_factor",
    spot_col="spot",
    out_col="forward",
)

forward_bad = ~np.isfinite(pd.to_numeric(clean_quotes["forward"], errors="coerce")) | (pd.to_numeric(clean_quotes["forward"], errors="coerce") <= 0)
forward_fallback = clean_quotes["spot"] * np.exp(clean_quotes["rate"].fillna(0.0) * clean_quotes["tau"].fillna(0.0))
clean_quotes.loc[forward_bad, "forward"] = forward_fallback.loc[forward_bad]
forward_report = pd.DataFrame([{"forward_fallback_share": float(forward_bad.mean()), "forward_fallback_rows": int(forward_bad.sum())}])

clean_quotes = infer_carry_from_forward(
    clean_quotes,
    spot_col="spot",
    forward_col="forward",
    tau_col="tau",
    out_col="implied_carry",
)
clean_quotes = infer_dividend_yield_from_forward(
    clean_quotes,
    rate_col="rate",
    carry_col="implied_carry",
    out_col="implied_dividend_yield",
)

iv_quotes = implied_vol_table(
    clean_quotes,
    price_cols=("bid", "mid", "ask"),
    option_type_col="option_type",
    spot_col="spot",
    forward_col="forward",
    strike_col="strike",
    tau_col="tau",
    rate_col="rate",
    discount_col="discount_factor",
    model="black76",
    engine=engine,
)
iv_quotes["iv_ok"] = iv_quotes["iv_mid_success"].fillna(False) & np.isfinite(iv_quotes["iv_mid"])
iv_quotes = compute_greeks_numpy(iv_quotes, iv_col="iv_mid")

surface_quotes = surface_ready_quotes(
    iv_quotes,
    min_iv=0.05,
    max_iv=3.50,

    max_tau=180 / 365.0,

    max_weight=20.0,
)
surface_quotes = add_calibration_weights(
    surface_quotes,
    price_uncertainty="half_spread",
    iv_uncertainty="spread_over_vega",

)

btc_calibration = calibration_quotes(
    surface_quotes,
    min_dte=3.0,
    max_dte=120.0,
    min_vega=0.0,
    max_relative_spread=0.85,
    otm_only=True,
)

main_date = choose_surface_date(
    btc_calibration,
    min_expiries=4,
    min_quotes=80,
    prefer_tail_coverage=True,
)
btc_day = btc_calibration.loc[btc_calibration["date"].eq(main_date)].copy()

btc_model_quotes = balanced_model_quotes(
    btc_day,
    target_dtes=(7, 14, 21, 30, 45, 60),
    target_ks=(-0.35, -0.25, -0.17, -0.10, -0.04, 0.00, 0.04, 0.10, 0.17, 0.25),
    min_quotes_per_expiry=6,
    prefer_tail_coverage=True,
)

btc_svi = fit_svi_surface(
    btc_day,
    weight_col="obs_weight",
    engine=engine,
)
btc_ssvi = fit_ssvi_surface(
    btc_day,
    weight_col="obs_weight",
    engine=engine,
)
btc_sabr = fit_sabr_surface(
    btc_day,
    betas=(1.0, 0.7, 0.5),
    primary_beta=1.0,
    weight_col="obs_weight",
    engine=engine,
)
btc_merton = fit_merton_jump_diffusion(
    btc_model_quotes,
    weight_col="obs_weight",
    engine=engine,
    max_nfev=45,
    fit_by_expiry=True,
)
btc_heston = fit_heston_mc(
    btc_model_quotes,
    paths_opt=2048,
    paths_final=8192,
    steps_per_year=52,
    random_method="antithetic",
    common_random_numbers=True,
    engine=engine,
    random_state=random_state,
    max_nfev=70,
)
btc_bates = fit_bates_mc(
    btc_model_quotes,
    heston_start=btc_heston,
    jump_start=btc_merton,
    paths_opt=2048,
    paths_final=8192,
    steps_per_year=52,
    random_method="antithetic",
    common_random_numbers=True,
    engine=engine,
    random_state=random_state,

)

btc_common_quotes = common_model_quotes(

model_comparison = compare_model_fits(

dates_for_signal = dates_for_signal[-120:]

btc_svi_daily = fit_svi_holdout(

btc_sabr_daily = fit_sabr_holdout(

    warm_start=True,

)

btc_fair_values = model_fair_values(

btc_scores = residual_scores(

btc_residual_schedule = residual_entry_schedule(

btc_matched_schedule = matched_option_schedule(

The BTC model comparison is different from SPX. On the selected BTC panel:

  • Merton has the lowest weighted IV RMSE, about 0.0048,
  • SVI is around 0.0156,
  • SABR is around 0.0182,
  • Bates is around 0.0213,
  • Heston is around 0.0369,
  • SSVI is weakest at about 0.0492.

This is economically interesting. For BTC, the pure jump-diffusion diagnostic is very strong on the common benchmark. That makes sense because BTC option smiles often price abrupt jumps and gap-like moves very heavily. A jump component can explain a lot of the surface shape that SPX explained through skewed equity crash demand and smoother stochastic variance.

SSVI struggles because BTC smiles are too irregular for a globally disciplined surface to fit tightly. Heston also struggles because continuous stochastic variance alone isn’t enough to match the jump-like shape in this panel.

BTC Residual Validation and Hedging Friction

The BTC residual validation table shows positive mean hedged P&L in most deciles, but the pattern is irregular. The highest \(z\) decile is negative, which fits the earlier warning that extreme crypto residuals can be contaminated by microstructure and jump risk.

The hedging table shows a deeper issue: delta hedging in BTC can reduce drawdown but also damage net P&L through trading costs and hedge losses. In the matched ATM case, unhedged P&L is positive while delta-hedged P&L is negative. That means the underlying directional exposure helped the unhedged result, and hedging removed that benefit while adding costs.

For residual trades, delta hedging also worsens total P&L, but it reduces daily volatility and drawdown. This creates a real strategy design choice. If the goal is pure option relative value, delta hedging is necessary. If the goal is total return, the unhedged exposure may dominate, but then the result is less about model residuals.

The BTC residual decile table is also different. Mean next hedged P&L is positive in most deciles, but the highest residual decile has negative mean P&L. That again warns us against blindly trading the most extreme residuals. In BTC, extreme residuals may be exactly where liquidity is weakest, marks are less reliable, or jump risk is most mismeasured.

The schedule has 41 residual entries and 41 matched entries. The BTC hedging comparison separates unhedged and delta-hedged versions:

  • matched ATM unhedged gains about $1,705,
  • matched ATM delta-hedged loses about $6,395,
  • residual selector unhedged loses about $560,
  • residual selector delta-hedged loses about $1,277.

Delta hedging reduces volatility and drawdown for BTC, but it also turns the matched unhedged profit into a loss because hedge costs and hedge P&L dominate. For residual trades, both unhedged and delta versions lose, but the delta version has smaller daily volatility and drawdown.

The BTC diagnostics show the reality of crypto option backtesting:

  • the residual run has missing option marks on some days,
  • the matched run has no missing marks in the displayed diagnostics,
  • the calendar is 24/7,
  • the contract size is 1,
  • valuation is USD equivalent,
  • both unhedged and delta strategies are run.

This matters because BTC isn’t just “SPX with another ticker.” The trading calendar, liquidity, surface shape, and jump behavior change the meaning of the same model residual.

The final multi-panel figure gives a compact visual summary: BTC quote map, smile term structure, SVI/SSVI/SABR fits, Merton tail fit, Heston convergence, Heston/Bates comparison, model runtime/error, residual deciles, and scheduled hedge comparison. The strongest interpretation is that jump-style models are more competitive in BTC than in SPX, but model residuals still need strict cost and validation gates before they become tradable.

BTC Model Ranking and Why the Smile Looks Different

The BTC repeat is useful because it puts the same volatility-modeling stack into a market with a very different risk structure. SPX options are dominated by institutional index hedging, crash insurance demand, and a long history of left-skew behavior. BTC options also price downside risk, but they add another layer: large jump moves, weekend gaps, liquidity differences across expiries, and a market where the underlying itself can move like a high-volatility growth asset and a macro liquidity proxy at the same time.

The model comparison reflects that difference. In the SPX run, SVI is the clean surface-marking core. It fits the dense SPX smile with very low IV error and gives a stable fair-value engine. In the BTC run, the Merton jump-diffusion becomes much more competitive on the benchmark error table. That makes economic sense: BTC return distributions often have abrupt large moves, and a jump component can explain tail option prices with fewer contortions than a smooth diffusion-only smile.

The practical reading is simple: BTC rewards jump-aware explanations more strongly than SPX does in this sample. SVI and SABR still matter because they give fast and flexible surface marks, but the jump model carries more information about the option cross-section than it did for SPX.

The cleaned BTC panel also tells us why the secondary application has to be interpreted carefully. The raw chain loses many rows through price, spread, DTE, and moneyness filters before we reach the final panel. That filtering is good research hygiene, but it also means the final comparison is based on the liquid and usable part of the BTC surface. We are modeling the tradable surface, not every quote shown by the venue.

BTC Residual Validation

The BTC residual decile table asks the same question as the SPX validation section: after a model marks a quote as cheap or rich, does that residual have any relationship with the next-period hedged payoff?

For each option observation, the residual is built as:

\[ z_i = \frac{V_i^{\text{model}} - V_i^{\text{mid}}}{\text{uncertainty}_i} \]

where \(V_i^{\text{model}}\) is the model fair value, \(V_i^{\text{mid}}\) is the market mid price, and the denominator combines quote noise, model disagreement, and fit uncertainty. A positive \(z_i\) means the model value is above the market mid after scaling by uncertainty, so the option looks cheap. A negative \(z_i\) means the model value is below the market mid, so the option looks rich.

The decile table doesn’t show a clean monotonic pattern across all buckets. Some middle deciles have strong average next-period payoffs, while the most extreme positive bucket is weaker. This is an important result. A residual can be mathematically large because the model is confident, because the quote is wide, because the tail is difficult, or because the option is genuinely mispriced. The validation step separates these possibilities by asking what happened afterward.

For BTC, the evidence is mixed rather than clean. There is useful information in the residuals, but the relationship is less stable than the surface error table alone would suggest. That’s why the secondary run uses scheduled trade tests instead of stopping at model fit. A model that fits the smile well still needs the residual to survive spreads, hedge noise, and the large realized volatility of the underlying.

BTC Scheduled Trades and Delta Hedging

The BTC scheduled-trade section compares two ways of entering option positions. The matched ATM strategy gives us a simple reference trade around the same date and maturity region, while the residual-selector strategy uses the model-risk-aware residual filter. Both are then evaluated with and without delta hedging.

A delta-hedged option position tries to remove the first-order exposure to BTC price moves. If the option position has delta \(\Delta_t\), the hedge holds approximately \(-\Delta_t\) units of BTC exposure:

\[ \Pi_t = V_t - \Delta_t S_t \]

The one-period change is approximately:

\[ \Delta \Pi_t \approx \underbrace{\Delta V_t - \Delta_t \Delta S_t}_{\text{delta-hedged option move}} - \underbrace{\text{costs}_t}_{\text{spreads and hedge trading}} \]

For a perfectly delta-neutral world with stable implied volatility and continuous rebalancing, the first-order BTC move would mostly disappear. In reality, BTC jumps, the hedge is discrete, spreads are meaningful, and the option surface itself moves. So the delta hedge reduces directional exposure, but it also adds hedge turnover and extra transaction costs.

The BTC results show exactly that tradeoff. The unhedged matched ATM run has positive total P&L in this sample, while the delta-hedged version turns negative after costs. That means the unhedged benchmark likely benefited from directional BTC moves or favorable option exposure, and the hedge removed part of that benefit while adding cost. The residual-selector trades are smaller and more selective, but they also struggle after costs.

This is a very useful outcome for a research notebook because it prevents a false conclusion. A model residual can look interesting in the surface, and a hedge can look theoretically cleaner, but the actual trading layer can still lose money once execution and discrete rebalancing are included.

BTC Diagnostic Counters

The diagnostic counters matter because they explain where the backtest mechanics are fragile. BTC options can disappear from the markable panel, shift liquidity across strikes, or reach the DTE exit before the fixed holding period completes. These events change how a clean theoretical trade becomes an actual backtest trade.

The matched ATM run has missing marks, while the residual-selector run has cleaner marking behavior. That difference is meaningful. A missing mark is a serious accounting and execution issue. The backtest couldn’t observe a reliable exit value for the contract on a scheduled day, so the realized trade path becomes less clean. In option strategies, missing marks often happen in the places where the surface is thinner, spreads are wider, or strikes move away from the active trading region.

The DTE exits also deserve attention. An option position close to expiry becomes extremely sensitive to small underlying moves because gamma increases as time shrinks. If the trade reaches the DTE stop, the backtest exits before the option becomes too short-dated and noisy. This is a realistic control because most systematic volatility strategies avoid holding tiny-dated options unless they are explicitly designed for short-gamma or event-volatility trading.

The final BTC hedge comparison therefore has to be read through three layers:

  • model layer: which model explains the surface best,
  • signal layer: whether residuals predict future option payoffs,
  • execution layer: whether marks, spreads, and hedge costs allow the signal to survive.

BTC performs well as a secondary stress test because it pressures all three layers at once. It has enough option data to run the workflow, but the market is still noisy enough that weak signals are punished quickly.

Secondary BTC Reading

The BTC section closes the workflow by showing that the full stack is reusable while the interpretation remains market-specific. The same cleaning logic, model comparison, residual scaling, validation, and scheduled-trade engine can run on BTC options, but the model ranking changes and the trading results become more sensitive to execution.

The most important BTC result is that jump-aware modeling becomes more valuable, while hedged residual trading remains difficult. Merton’s strong benchmark fit says the BTC smile contains jump-like information. The residual validation says that model mispricing signals exist but aren’t uniformly clean across deciles. The hedge comparison says that removing directional BTC exposure can reduce drawdown in some places, but the extra costs can dominate the benefit.

That gives the secondary run a clear economic interpretation. BTC options are rich enough for advanced volatility modeling, but the trading edge is harder than the model fit. The surface can be explained; the residual can be ranked; the trade can still fail after costs. That final separation between model fit, signal value, and tradable P&L is the main lesson from the BTC implementation.
